Types of data analytics include:
Descriptive data analytics, which describes and answers
questions about what has happened over a period of time.
It can help to keep track of business successes and failures
as well as providing essential insights into past business
performance. For example, data can be used to describe
what has happened to a firm's sales revenues over a given
period of time.
Diagnostic data analytics, which focuses on and answers
questions about why something has happened. It goes
beyond finding out what has happened by determining the
cause and examining why it has happened. For example, to
determine the extent to which a promotional campaign or
change in pricing method has impacted sales volume.
Predictive data analytics, which projects and answers
questions about what is likely to happen in the foreseeable
future. For example, this approach enables managers to
extrapolate data and make more realistic sales forecasts by
using historical data to identify trends. Such techniques
include the use of simple linear regression (see Chapter 58).
Prescriptive data analytics, which supports strategic
planning and an appropriate course of action by answering
questions about what should be done. For example, if data
analytics suggests a high likelihood of warmer summer
evenings, restaurants may need to order more food and
drinks, as well as hire more staff in anticipation of more
diners.
Essentially, data analytics is important because it helps
businesses to improve their efficiency, cut costs and gain
competitive advantages in order to increase their profits. It
enables businesses to gain insights that were not previously
accessible in order to establish new patterns and correlations
in large data sets. Data-driven decisions are more objective (as
they are based on evidence) so help to reduce risks. Having large
amounts of data and relevant information enables businesses
to improve their performance, such as helping to identify
consumer trends and raising customer satisfaction by providing
new and better-quality goods and services. Ultimately, data
analytics can be used to make more informed business decisions
notwithstanding uncertainties in the economy.
Database (A01)

A database is a computerized system that makes it easy to store,
search and select data and information. In the same way that a
public library stores a large range of books, a database stores a
large volume of data and information that is used by a business.
With computerised systems and structures, businesses can
input, organize, save, protect and retrieve data in an efficient
way (in terms of speed and accuracy).
Businesses will typically use databases to keep track of
information about customers, employees, inventory (stock)
and accounting information. For example, a shoe retailer that
sells a range of different types of footwear will need to keep
records of the sales of the different shoes sold (such as the type,
size and colour of the shoes) as well as important details about
the customers. Similarly, schools are likely to use a database to
keep track of each student's personal details, such as their name,
age, year group, home address, details of the parents or legal
guardians, medical records, attendance and punctuality records
and emergency contact details. Schools will also have a similar
database for their staff, as well as records of their ongoing
professional training and career development.
In the digital age, the disadvantages of using databases are
minimal, but include the initial set-up costs as well as ongoing
maintenance costs, such as the cost of hiring database managers.
There is also the potential risk of cybersecurity (see below).
Nevertheless, the reliance of businesses on accurate financial
records, secure credit card accounts, efficient billing and
invoicing and important customer records are all valid reasons
why databases are so important for businesses.

5.9 Management information systems (HL only)

Cybersecurity and cybercrime

(A01)

Cybersecurity refers to the protection of computer systems and
networks from unwarranted information disclosure, as well as
theft of or damage to computer hardware, software or data. It is
used to protect businesses and individuals against cybercrime.

Cybercrime refers to any illegal activity carried out using
computers or the Internet by deliberately and maliciously
targeting computers, computer networks or networked devices.
Cybercrime can be carried out by individuals or organizations
and is usually done for financial reasons (profit), but in some
cases can be caused by political or personal motives.

With the increased reliance on e-commerce and the growing
popularity of a cashless society, cybercrime is becoming more Figure 43.2 - Cybersecurity is an increasingly important issue
of a threat to people and businesses across the world. Examples for businesses
of interrelated cybercrime include:

Phishing - This is the use of fraudulent messages designed
by the attacker to trick victims into revealing sensitive
information.
Ransomware - This is the use of malicious software from
cybercriminals who threaten to publish the victim's
personal data or permanently block access to the data
unless a ransom is paid to the attackers.
Email and internet fraud - This refers to the use of enticing
messages in emails and text messages, such as "Tap on this
link and claim your $1 million today!"
Identity theft - This occurs when an individual's private
information is stolen and used without any permission.
Account hijacking - This occurs when an individual's
private or profession account (such as email, social media
or bank account) is stolen and abused or misused. This
includes hijacking a company's website and shutting it
down completely.
Intellectual property theft - This is the piracy or theft of
materials that legally belong to others, such as copyright
infringements and counterfeiting of registered trademarks
(see Chapter 42).
Businesses can protect themselves against cybercrimes by
improving their cybersecurity systems and processes. This
includes methods such as:
Keeping computer software, network structures and
operating system updated.
Using anti-virus software to prevent or limit the volume of
cyberattacks.
Training staff about the importance of cybersecurity and
practical strategies such as:
o never opening unsolicited email attachments
o using stronger security passwords (and updating these
at appropriate times) and
o being extremely cautious when disclosing private or
confidential information.

Critical infrastructures
Critical infrastructures, including (i) artificial neural networks, (ii)
data centres and (iii) cloud computing. AO2
© IBO, 2022
C

ritical infrastructure refers to the essential and
interrelated physical structures and facilities needed
for the effective functioning of a business. These
include, but are not limited to, (i) artificial neural networks, (ii)
data centres and (iii) cloud computing.
{i} Artificial neural networks

Artificial neural networks (ANN) are a form of machine-
learning that use learning algorithms that can independently
make adjustments as they receive new input. This means that
ANNs can solve problems without having to be explicitly
programmed with rules to follow, in a similar way to that of the
human brain. This means ANNs are the basic building blocks of
artificial intelligence (AI).
ANNs can be used for many business applications, such as
natural language processing in chatbots (used for interacting
online with customers) and predictive analysis for detecting
spam email and phishing text messages.
Inspired by the structure of the human brain, artificial neural
networks are used to make computers or machines more
human like in terms of their use of reasoning, intuition and
even imagination. ANNs were first developed back in the 1950s
to address the issue that computers cannot interpret the context
of real-world situations or apply common sense to problems in
the way that human brains are capable of.
Examples of business applications of artificial neural networks
include:
Google uses ANN learning algorithms to make its 'watch
next' recommendations for YouTube videos.
Facebook uses ANNs for its DeepFace facial recognition
system, which uses algorithms to recognize faces with
around 97% accuracy.
Microsoft's Skype uses ANN to do translations of live
online conversations.
chatbot
Figure 43.3 - Chatbots are used by an increasing number of
retail businesses
{ii} Data centres
A data centre is a physical facility or space of networked
computers and component resources that supports businesses
in housing their critical applications and data. The main
components of a data centre include routers, firewalls, secured
storage systems, mainframe servers and application-delivery
controllers.
Most businesses rely heavily on data for their day-to-day
operations, regardless of the industry or nature of the data. Data
centres enable a large volume of data to be stored, organized,
processed and distributed by businesses. Services provided
by data centres to support business applications and activities
include:
Data backup and archiving of important files, documents
and records.
Email and file sharing
Database systems
Big data, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning
Virtual communications and collaboration services.
All of this means that data centres are vital to the continuity of
Commercial banks, such as HSBC, use chatbots to deal a business as they house an organization's critical and valuable
with customer queries in real-time. assets needed for its daily operations. The world's largest data
centre is the Citadel Campus at Tahoe Reno Industrial Centre
5.9 Management information systems (HL only)

(TRIC), located in Nevada, US. The data centre is spread over
1,000 acres and has up to 7.2 million square feet of data centre
space.

Figure 43.4 - Data centres are used by businesses in every
industry
{iii) Cloud computing

Cloud computing is similar to data centres except that it is a
virtual resource or online space that enables businesses to store,
organize and retrieve data in safe and efficient ways. As with
data centres, cloud computing requires the use of computer
networks and remote servers, which possess a unique function.

However, there has been a shift in critical infrastructure from
traditional on-premises physical servers in data centres to virtual
networks that support work applications and data management
in a cloud environment. The 'cloud' is not a physical entity but
a virtual service and is accessed via an Internet connection. At
the most basic level, cloud computing storage services include
Google Drive, Microsoft One Drive, iCloud and Dropbox.
Other examples of cloud services providers for businesses
include Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft (Azure) and
IBM Cloud. Some of the differences between data centres and
cloud computing are outlined in Table 43.1 below.

Table 43.1 - Data centres versus cloud computing

A physical resource that helps businesses to store, organize and
retrieve data in an efficient and safe way.
The investment costs are significant compared with cloud
computing.
Maintenance costs are high, including hardware engineers,
developers, security and temperature monitoring systems.
It does not rely on having Internet or Wi-Fi connections, as
Ethernet cables are used.

Virtual reality (A02}

Virtual reality comes from the words "virtual" (meaning near)
and "reality" (meaning what we experience as human beings).
Hence, virtual reality (VR) means near-reality. It an artificial,
three-dimensional environment that is created with software
and presented to the user in a near-reality way that people
can explore and interact with. VR technologies enable users to
experience things through the senses of sight and sound in a
three-dimensional and interactive environment.
VR has both entertainment and commercial use. It is
,.. commonplace in the corporate world. For example, airline
Ill c C a, companies use VR technologies to create computer generated
.2 'la E g, virtual environments for flight simulations used to train and test
t ~ pilots. This creates a realistic, albeit safe, environment for pilots
8" E training to handle potential hazards and challenges during
a flight, such as adverse weather conditions and emergency
landing protocols.

pilots
With VR becoming cheaper and more widespread, analysts
expect to see many more possibilities and uses for the
technology in the future. Examples of the use ofVR in education
are outlined in Box 43.1. Nevertheless, the set-up costs can still
prove to be expensive, especially if the content needs to be
customized and engaging.

to incur the expenses and inconveniences associated

5.9 Management information systems (HL only)

operate within the law governing the collection, storage and
The Internet of Things (loT) refers to a broad system of transfer or sharing of data.
physical objects embedded with electronics, software and
sensors that connect to the Internet. These devices are able
to collect, transfer and store huge volumes of data over the
Internet in real time. Hence, the physical objects ( or 'things')
are also referred to connected devices through wireless and
Bluetooth technologies. Examples include smart devices (such
as smartphones, smart heating systems, office security devices
and home appliances) as well as wearable technologies.

Figure 43.7 - The Internet of things has unlimited
applications for businesses
For example, in the healthcare industry, wearable smart devices
are an application of the IoT. They can be used to keep records
of health-related data for health clinics, hospitals and health
insurance providers. Doctors or surgeons, for example, can use
a large volume of statistical data of their patients so that the best
form of treatment can be applied in a timely manner.

Car manufacturers and car dealerships use data from each vehicle
to offer customers an appointment for servicing (maintenance),
to get their parts fixed, send customers directions to the nearest
dealer or garage and make sure the correct replacement parts
are ordered so they are ready for when the customer arrives.
Hence, the loT helps businesses to operate in a more lean and
efficient way (see Chapter 37) and can generate significant
competitive advantages.

The purpose behind the Internet of Things is for connected
devices that self-report in real-time so that the data can be
used to improve efficiency. It removes the need to depend on
human intervention to collect, process and interpret important
information. Moreover, the loT is able to do this far more
quickly and accurately, in real-time.

The Internet of Things generates massive volumes of data
from countless devices that are permanently connected to the
Internet. The personal and business possibilities of this are only
limited by imagination and creativity. However, due to the vast

Case study 43.1 - Smart devices

Amazon's Alexa, Google's Home and Apple's Siri (digital
voice assistants) are examples of widely used consumer
loT applications that are increasingly integral to the daily
lives of billions of people. Users can talk to digital voice
assistants like Alexa for a wide and growing variety of
functions including playing music on demand, reporting
live news coverage, providing weather reports, asking
questions about literally any topic, calling family and
friends, setting reminders and alarms, ordering an Uber
and so much more.
The main advantage of the loT is that it improves efficiency
(minimizing human effort and saving time to get tasks done).
Enhanced data collection and access to real-time information
also help with rational decision making. However, the main
concerns evolve around the issue of data security and privacy
concerns. There could also be concerns about the growing
dependency on the Internet and hence the inability for
businesses to function efficiently without it.
Artificial intelligence (A02)
Artificial intelligence (AI) is an aspect of computer science
that focuses on the ability of smart machines to perform
tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as voice
commands on a smartphone or in a car. AI enables intelligent
machines to work and react like humans. However, AI has the
ability to boost operational efficiency and complete highly
complex tasks that cannot be easily managed by human beings.

Hence, AI provides many opportunities for businesses to boost
productivity in cost-effective ways.
For example, AI is commonly used in the car manufacturing
industry. Satellite navigation, with global positioning systems,
automatically gather, process and evaluate real-time driving
conditions for motorists, helping them to follow the optimum
route with AI guidance to help avoid congested roads as well as
other road hazards. An increasing number of car manufacturers
are using AI to develop and produce autonomous vehicles (AV)
that are self-driving. Such vehicles are equipped with multiple
sensors, such as cameras, radars and lidar ( used to calculate
., ranges and variable distance for speed and breaking). These

Figure 43.8 - Autonomous vehicles rely on Al technologies
Other examples of the use of artificial intelligence in the
business world include:
Human resource management - Artificial Intelligence is
being increasingly used for hiring (recruiting) workers.
With hundreds of candidates potentially applying for a
single vacancy in an organization, many businesses use
AI and language processing software to filter through
the curricula vitae (resumes) and shortlist the suitable
candidates who meet the employer's requirements. This
is done by analyzing different attributes of the candidates
(such as their skills, experience and qualifications) in line
with the job description and person's specifications.
Cybersecurity - This is one of the most important
applications of AI for businesses. Given the reliance on
online technologies, such as the storage of important
databases of financial data, business plans, private
information about employees and so forth, the use of AI to
understand, detect and remove unwanted cyber threats is
paramount to the operations of businesses.
Data analysis - AI enables businesses to collect and process
a huge amount of data to provide feedback and predictions
about changing customer needs and preferences. This
enables the business to provide better customer experiences
and marketing strategies that engage customers and build
brand loyalty. For example, social media platforms use
targeted adverts based on the massive volume of data
collected from people's smartphones and mobile devices.
Financial management - Artificial Intelligence has
made financial management much easier for businesses
by automating billing and invoicing systems and the
subsequent recording of financial data. Electronic invoices
and financial filing are easier to handle (and far more
efficient than manual data input systems). For example,
many small businesses have benefited from the use of AI
technologies from providers such as PayPal to automate
payment systems as well as provide data analytics to
support financial planning.
Automated customer services - The use of AI and machine
learning can improve customer engagement and improve
the quality of services without the need to hire so many
workers. For example, AI allows search engines to be
smarter and online chatbots used by banks and retailers to
be more helpful in meeting the needs of customers.
Case study 43.2 - Hellenic Post

In 2022, Hellenic Post, the state-owned provider of postal
services in Greece, launched a fleet of 55 postal robots
to speed up its sorting and delivery services. Using Al
technologies, the four-wheeled autonomous mobile
robots scan the postal code on up to 168,000 parcels
weighing a maximum of 15kg each day. Directed by
sensors, the robots sort the parcels and deliver these
into the corresponding mail sacks set up around Hellenic
Post's sorting office. Up to 80% of Hellenic Post's parcel
sorting has been handed over to these robots.

and developing AI in the corporate world, it can be a highly
expensive investment. Critics are also doubtful about the
potential misuse of artificial intelligence as well as the impact
on employment in many sectors of the economy.

Big data (A02)

Businesses have huge potential to harness big data in digital Businesses use big data in several ways. Some examples include:
format to help them to understand their customers better.

Data sets are very important for any business as they can help
firms to enhance their marketing strategies, such as advertising
campaigns that target the right customers in the right way.
Big data can also enable businesses to offer a more bespoke
(personalised) service to meet the needs and preferences of
their clients.

There are many reasons for the exponential growth in big data,
including the data gathered from:

E-commerce, such data collected from shopping carts and
online purchases.
Use of logistics and transportation systems that use
electronic ticketing systems and location data using GPS
technologies (global positioning system).
Social media data, from interactions on platforms such
as Facebook, Instagram, Linkedln, Snapchat, Twitter and
WhatsApp.
The Internet of Things (IoT), such as data generating from
smartphones, mobile apps and smart appliances in the
home or office.
Hence, big data and data analytics are significant for the growth
and development of any business organization, which supports
the business in optimizing its performance. As stated by Angela
Ahrendts, Apple's former Senior Vice President, "Consumer
data will be the biggest differentiator ... whoever unlocks the
reams of data and uses it strategically will win''. Similarly, Ginni
Rometty, former CEO of IBM, said "Big data will spell the death
of customer segmentation and force the marketer to understand
each customer as an individual."

Generating marketing insights - Big data can generate
important insights to the changing needs and wants of
customers, based on data gathered e-commerce data
analytics and social media posts, for example. Big data has
revolutionized traditional methods of market research (see
Chapter 26).
Tracking and monitoring - Access to big data helps a
business to have better control over its operations. For
example, transportation companies use big data for
capacity management, which is also important for ensuring
the safety of their customers. Hence, big data can help
businesses to improve their overall efficiency and financial
performance.
Improved decision-making -Big data enables businesses to
use and analyse information in real-time to aid decision
making. For example, airline companies and mobility
service providers (such as Uber) use big data for dynamic
pricing strategies (see Chapter 28) as well as for other
elements of the marketing mix (see Chapters 27 - 33).

Customer loyalty programmes
(A03)
A customer loyalty programme refers to any customer-
retention strategy that incentivizes customers to continue
buying the same products and brands of the business, instead
of switching to those provided by competitors. They are used
to encourage repeat purchases by using different reward
programmes. For example, reward points accumulated on
loyalty schemes can be redeemed for special discounts or gifts.
Some customer loyalty programmes are so successful that they
have become a long-term strategy to promote an organization's
products or brands, such as airline frequent flyer programmes
or customer loyalty programmes used by supermarket chains.
Customer loyalty programmes are a marketing approach
designed to improve customer relationships and to ensure both
Figure 43.10 - Many businesses use subscriptions to
retain their customer base
The most basic form of loyalty programmes offers customers
greater rewards based on the value or volume of purchases or
visits made, such as a clothes retailer, theme park or cinema.
Many airline companies offer frequent flyer programmes whilst
hotel chains offer loyalty points based on the amount spent by
parties feel that they are getting something beneficial from this. customers. Amazon Prime customers, who pay for the privilege,
So, customers provide their ongoing support by making repeat enjoy membership benefits such as free shipping and digital.
purchases or engaging with a brand on a recurring basis. In media streaming services.
return for their loyalty, customers receive loyalty rewards, such
as discounts, rewards coupons or freebies (free gifts).
The main argument for using customer loyalty programmes,
despite their cost, is that the spending to retain customers is
far cheaper than the spending needed to attract new customers.
Loyalty programmes tend to work because they make customers
feel special and valued, which further leads to customer
retention, more referrals (word of mouth recommendations)
and therefore higher profits in the long term.
By contrast, without a loyalty programme, customers might
simply walk away permanently, meaning the business loses
this revenue stream forever. Winning the loyalty of customers
is so important that many businesses have switched to using
a subscription model to collect reoccurring payments from
customers. For services, customers get new content on a regular
basis (such as in the case of Netflix or InThinking Business
Management). In the case of goods, loyal customers must feel
they get value for money (such as in the case of coffee shops that
use subscription models). Subscribers represent customers who
have pledged their allegiance to the business.
For customer loyalty programmes to work, a huge amount of
data is needed to ensure the rewards reflect what customers
actually want and that the costs of operating the rewards
programme does not outweigh the benefits. This requires
businesses to collect, process and store data, such as customer
spending habits (like the most frequently bought items, the
frequency of purchases per time period and the average spend
per transaction). It may also include gathering regular feedback
from customers. This data enables businesses to determine
the best marketing strategies to use to target, entice and retain
customers. Listening to customers is important not only to be
able to develop sustainable loyalty programmes, but also to
improve the overall customer experience so as to establish a
loyal customer base.

Taylorism is based on developing policies and practices
that maximize efficiency and productivity by standardizing
work processes and techniques for completing each task.
Digital Taylorism is found in organizations that use data and
surveillance (monitoring) systems to monitor employees to
ensure they remain on task at all times. The number of firms
using such systems is continually growing. The Economist has
described Amazon and FedEx as a digital Taylorism corporate
culture, arguing that "what gets measured, gets managed:'

Common methods of staff monitoring systems include software
monitoring (to track what employees are doing on their
computers), telephone recordings, video surveillance, email
monitoring and location monitoring. Electronic monitoring
systems and digital tools to gather data provide managers
with the ability to continuously evaluate and measure the
performance of employees, irrespective of whether they are in
the office or working from home. There are plenty of options
available to businesses, including a growing number of online
staff monitoring apps such as Workpuls (https:/ /www.workpuls.
com), which specializes in data analytics for workforce
productivity.

individual managers to have complete oversight of every

systems to collect the data needed to monitor and support

Improved coordination and control -Using data and staff
monitoring systems enables employers to know everything
that is going on in their business at all times. This includes
identifying areas where workers need to improve their
performance as well as spotting employees who might
be violating company policies. There will always be
dishonest people in the workplace, especially in very large
organizations that have many employees.
Training and development- Data used to monitor employees
can be used to fix mistakes and to improve performance.
For example, most 1B World Schools use examination data
to inform school leaders about the quality of teaching and
learning. Teachers are recognized for their areas of strength
and supported in areas that may need some improvement
or development.
Improved productivity and efficiency -People tend to be
more focused on their work and less distracted if they know
they are being monitored. For example, you might notice
a slightly different approach and attitude of educators
when by they are being observed by senior management.
In theory, the data and information collated from such
observations helps to improve the overall productivity in
the workplace.
To reward employees - As with any form of scientific
management, digital Taylorism rewards more productive
workers who meet or exceed targets. for example,
data can reveal which individual employees or teams
have contributed the most to the firm's sales revenue.
Furthermore, monitoring systems can provide evidence of
the many instances when employees go above and beyond
what is expected of them.

Data mining is a particularly useful technique to support a
firm's marketing competitiveness. For example, a common use
of data mining is to break down the vast amount of data about
customers into meaningful segments such as age, gender, race,
income and occupation. Ultimately, data mining is used to help
managers to make more-informed business decisions. Data
mining has many business applications, such as:
Consumer profiling - to examine customer purchasing
patterns and making connections of the data to consumer
demographics (see Chapter 24) in order to make better
marketing decisions.
Marketing planning -using meaningful data to inform a
business about its segmentation, targeting and positioning
strategies (see Chapter 24).
Sales forecasting -to identify sales trends and to make
accurate sales predictions based on data about customer
spending habits (see Chapter 25).
Market research - to develop improved marketing
campaigns (see Chapter 26). Data mining can be used to
predict what customers might want to purchase in the
future, based on data collected about their past purchasing
habits (see Case study 43.3 below).
5.9 Management information systems (HL only)

Customer loyalty schemes -businesses such as supermarkets
use mined data to retain customers by developing
appropriate reward programmes.
Market basket analysis - retailers use data mining
techniques to gain a better understanding of customer
purchasing patterns based on items purchased in the past
or items placed in a basket (on an e-commerce platform).
Production planning -to support smart inventory control
systems as well as to identify any gaps and errors in
production processes, such as bottlenecks in supply chains
(see Chapter 40).
Research and development -to inform R&D expenditure,
product development and innovation strategies based on
the predicted needs and preferences of customers (see
Chapter 42).

Case study 43.3 - Walmart, Hurricanes and
Strawberry Pop-Tarts

So, what do Walmart, Hurricanes and Strawberry pop
tarts all have in common? It is common for households
to panic buy essential grocery items (such as milk, bread,
rice, potatoes and eggs) when there are announcements
made about imminent severe weather conditions.
However, according to data mining by Walmart in 2017,
customers in the US also purchase up to seven times more
Strawberry Pop-Tarts ahead of a hurricane. Walmart Said
that Strawberry Pop-Tarts are one of the pre-hurricane
top-selling food items as they do not require heating, can
be eaten at any meal and have a long shelf life. Walmart
has used data mining and predictive technologies since

Case study 43.4 - Data mining and
customer loyalty programmes
Retailers such as supermarkets are established users of
data mining techniques. Many supermarkets offer free
loyalty programmes to customers. Loyalty cards are used
to offer customers reduced prices and special offers that
are not available to non-members. The magnetic strips
on customer loyalty cards make it easy for retailers to
track what customers are buying, the quantities in which
they buy these, when they are buying the products and
at what price. After mining the data, supermarket stores
can then use this information to execute more suitable
marketing strategies to target and retain their customers.
However, the use of data mining has come under scrutiny
and criticism especially when users, employees or customers
are unaware of their data being collected and mined, often
for commercial gain. The selling, sharing or redistribution of
personal information without the prior knowledge and approval
of owners is unethical and illegal in many countries, especially
when the data are used to influence preferences and decision
making. For example, numerous social media companies have
been severely criticized for using data mining techniques to
generate profits.
Nevertheless, data mining enables a vast amount of useful
information to help businesses to increase their sales
revenues, cut costs, improve customer relations management
and reduce risks. As stated by Carly Fiorina, former CEO of
Hewlett-Packard, "The goal is to turn data into information
and information into insight." Essentially then, data mining is a
powerful tool for increasing the profits of a business.

Management Information Systems
(MIS)
The benefits, risks and ethical implications of advanced computer
technologies (collectively referred to here as Management
Information Systems) and technological innovation on business
decision making and stakeholders. (A03)
© IBO, 2022
M

anagement Information Systems (MIS) refers
to the study of advanced computer technologies
and their impact on organizations, people and the
relationships among them. It is about people, processes and
technology in an organizational context. MIS covers the entire
contents of this chapter: data analytics, databases, cybersecurity
and cybercrime, critical infrastructures (including artificial
neural networks, data centres and cloud computing), virtual
reality, the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, big data,
customer loyalty programmes and the use of data to manage
and monitor employees (digital Taylorism).
The advantages of MIS have been outlined in the various
sections of this chapter. If set up and used appropriately, a
Management Information System enables businesses to have
better coordination, control, analysis and visualization of data
and information relevant to the operations of the organization.
Ultimately, the use of MIS enables managers to make better
informed decisions by having flexible and speedy access to
accurate data in order to achieve the goals and objectives of the
organization.
However, the opposite in the use and over reliance of MIS
in business organizations. examples include hardware and
software failure, cybercrime and data privacy. The monitoring
of employees in the workplace can be controversial and may
cause conflict between employers and employees because
both stakeholder groups try to protect their personal interests.
Employees want to maintain their privacy while employers
want to ensure workers don't abuse their privileges or misuse
(waste) the firm's scarce and valuable resources. To minimize
the potential conflict, businesses can ensure their Management
Information Systems, such as staff monitoring policies and
practices, are implemented in transparent, indiscriminate and
ethical ways. For example, organizations that opt to monitor
their employees' online activities can install software on work
computers and mobile devices that block access to specific
websites (such as online gaming sites) or restricts the amount
of time that employees can spend on certain Internet sites that
are not directly related to their jobs.
Employers can establish respect for the privacy of their
employees by creating clear policies that define the parameters
of acceptable and unacceptable uses of company computers and
other devices or equipment. The policies should also specify
the organization's right to monitor the work of employees,
including online activities, as well as the consequences for
violating the rules.
As previously mentioned, monitoring employees in secret or
even outside of work hours, without their prior knowledge or
permission is unethical and likely to be illegal. The same applies
to the monitoring and surveillance of customers. Collecting
and storing personal data of customers and employees that an
organization does not actually need in order to function as a
business entity also raises ethical questions about the (mis)use
of Management Information Systems in the corporate world.
Figure 43.13 - How do we determine whether it is ethical
to monitor the work of employees?

Question 43.1 - Meta
In early 2022, Meta was accused of abusing its market dominance in the UK to sell personal data of its 44 million Facebook
users. This led to a multi-million-dollar lawsuit against the social media giant. The litigation case came only several months
after the US Federal Trade Commission was given the go-ahead to take Meta to court over antitrust rules used to protect
consumers by blocking monopolies that take advantage of their customers.
UK laws protect individuals from being harmed in any way, financially or otherwise, caused by Management Information
Systems such as Internet of Things (loT) and artificial intelligence (Al) to mine personal data. In response to the
accusations, Facebook said its users have "meaningful control" of what data and information they choose to share on the
social media platform.

Each of the fifteen tools in the BMT can be classified in three
ways: (i) situational tools, (ii) planning tools or (iii) decision-
making tools.

Situational tools are used to assist managers and
entrepreneurs to assess aspects of the internal and external
factors affecting their business. Examples of such tools
Decision-making tools are used to assist managers and
entrepreneurs to make informed choices and judgements
by considering different quantitative and/or qualitative
factors. Decision making is a key role of managers and
entrepreneurs. Examples of decision-making tools include
the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix and the
Ansoff matrix. Decision-making tools help managers and
entrepreneurs to address the question "How do we get
there?"
Note: It is not always helpful nor necessary to classify the tools
in the above ways because the BMT may have overlapping
applications to the contents of the course. Hence, it is possible
that a particular tool can apply to more than one of the above
classifications.
Top Tip!

Managers and entrepreneurs have good judgement.
Sometimes, this judgment is due to their intuition (or
gut feeling), which is often based on their experience,
expertise, and/or personal preferences. Intuitive
decision-making can lead to quick decisions being
made. However, for more strategic decisions, relying
only on intuition can be highly risky as the choices
are not necessarily supported by any research or
data. Hence, managers and entrepreneurs often use
a variety of BMT to ensure their decision making is
objective, rational and logical. This is referred to as
scientific decision-making. This helps to reduce the risks
of making mistakes.

Planning tools are used to assist managers and
entrepreneurs to prepare and implement specific projects
and developments. Examples of such tools include business
plans, Gantt charts (HL only) and critical path analysis
(HL only). Such tools help managers and entrepreneurs
to organise resources efficiently and to complete a project
or business venture on time. Planning tools help decision

SWOT analysis considers the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of a
business at a specific point in time. Strengths and weaknesses are internal factors that
influence the business, while opportunities and threats are external factors which the
business has no direct control over.
The Ansoff matrix is a framework of generic growth strategies for a business, based on
providing new or existing products in new or existing markets. These four generic growth
strategies are categorised as (i) market penetration, (ii) market development, (iii) product
development and (iv) diversification.
This framework considers factors in the external environment that affect a business.
STEEPLE refers to the social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and
ethical aspects of the external environment. It provides an overview of or insight into
these external factors that are largely beyond the control of the organization.
The Boston Consulting Group (BCG) matrix allows managers to assess their organization's
product portfolio based on measures of relative market share and market growth. It
helps with long-term strategic planning and decision-making based on four categories of
products: (i) question marks, (ii) stars, (iii) cash cows and (iv) dogs.
This is an official guiding document that provides details of the organization's strategic
goals and how the business intends to achieve these, with reference to the firm's human
resources, finances, marketing and operations management. It is also commonly used to
secure loans from financial lenders as well as raising finance from investors.

Business Management Toolkit (BMT) 1

SWOT Analysis)
"The greatest glory in living lies not in never failing, but in rising every time we fail."
Nelson Mandela (1918 - 2013), President of South Africa 1994 to 1999r
SWOT analysis
The Business Management toolkit is a set of
situational, planning and decision-making tools
used to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content
as well as being applied in different contexts. SWOT
analysis is a situation tool. Chapter references have been included
as suggestions to show where SWOT analysis can be applied in
various parts of the syllabus.
© 180, 2022
Figure 44.1 - SWOT analysis is a commonly used situational
tool
SWOT analysis is a situational tool used to assess the internal
strengths and weaknesses and the external opportunities and
threats of a business. SWOT is an acronym for Strengths,
Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats. It can be used to
assess the current situation of a business or organization.
SWOT analysis considers both internal factors (strengths and

weaknesses) and external factors (opportunities and threats)
that are relevant to the organization under consideration.
Strengths are internal factors that are favourable compared
with competitors, such as strong brand loyalty, a good
corporate image or highly skilled workers. Strengths help
the business to better achieve its organizational objectives
(see Chapter 3). Hence, strengths need to be developed and
protected.
Weaknesses are internal factors that are unfavourable
when compared to rivals. Such factors create competitive
disadvantages. Weaknesses are therefore likely to prevent
or delay the business from achieving its goals. Hence,
to remain competitive, the business needs to reduce or
remove its weaknesses.
Opportunities are the external possibilities (prospects)
for future development. Such factors refer to changes in
the external environment that create favourable conditions
for a business. For example, India and China present
many business opportunities for multinational companies
(see Chapter 6), such as a huge customer base and rapid
economic growth. Hence, SWOT analysis can help
organizations to formulate their business strategies.
Threats are the external factors that hinder the prospects
for an organization. Hence, threats cause problems for the
business. Examples include technological breakdowns,
product defects and recalls (see Chapter 40), changes in
fashion, price wars (Chapter 28), oil crises, recessions,
natural disasters and the outbreak of infectious diseases.
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Table 1 .3.d SWOT analysis template (illustrative example)*

Strengths Weaknesses
. Unique selling point. Limited revenue streams
. Brand awareness and brand loyalty. Escalating costs of production
. Experience, knowledge and skills. Poor cash flow/ liquidity problems
. Market share/ market dominance. Higher prices than closest rivals
. Corporate image and brand reputation. Demotivated and/or unproductive workforce
. Accreditation, endorsement or official support. Limited sources of finance
. Core competencies, e.g., product quality. Lack of spare capacity
. Geographical location. Restricted product range
. Value for money (quality in relation to price). Poor location

Opportunities Threats
. Economic growth/ upswing in the business cycle. New entrants in the marketplace
. Trade liberalization (government policies). Economic downturn (recession)
. Weakening exchange rate. Inflation (causing higher production costs)
. Technological developments. Pressure group action, e.g., protests
. Advancements in infrastructure. Social, environmental and legal constraints
. Market growth. Negative media coverage and publicity
. New markets and locations. Unfavourable changes in seasons and weather
. Demographic and social lifestyle changes. Adverse changes in fashion and tastes
. Government spending programmes. Crises, e.g. natural disasters or power shortages
. Mergers and acquisitions of rival firms

Note: what might be a strength for one business, such as its brand reputation or human capital, might actually be a weakness for
another organization. Equally, some threats, such as a change in weather or climate, might also be considered as opportunities for
other businesses.
Question 44.1 - Kidzplay Bouncy Castles

Kidzplay Bouncy Castles is a private limited company that
operates in a niche market, catering for children's parties and
events in London, UK. Outline whether each of the following
scenarios represent a strength, weakness, opportunity or
threat to Kidzplay Bouncy Castles.
(a) Limited competition in a niche market. [2marks)
(b) Limited marketing on its new website [2marks)
(c) Issues of recruiting and retaining staff. [2marks)
(d) Demand in the winter months is low. [2 marks)
(e) Large profit margins could attract new competitors.
[2 marks)
Exam tip!

When carrying out a SWOT analysis, remember that:
Strengths and weaknesses are the internal factors
that an organization currently faces.
Opportunities and threats are the external factors that
the organization is likely to face in the foreseeable
future.
Developing business strategies
based on SWOT analyses
SWOT analysis can be an extremely useful situational tool for
investigating all sorts of business situations as part of strategic
planning and decision making. For example, it can be used to
provide a framework for:

Competitor analysis, such as the threats posed by a
competitor or the strengths of a rival.
Assessing opportunities, such as the development and
growth prospects for the organization.
Risk assessment, such as the probable effects of investing in
a certain project or location.
Reviewing corporate strategy, such as the market position or
strategic direction of the business.
Strategic planning, such as the decision to diversify or
expand in oversea markets.
Once a SWOT analysis is completed, appropriate business
strategies can be identified and discussed to deal with potential
situations in a more optimal way based on the organization's
identified strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats. In
particular, organizations should strive to:

Build on their organizational strengths.
Reverse their weaknesses.
Maximize their responses to business opportunities.
Overcome threats to their businesses.
BMT 1 - SWOT Analysis

Just investigating the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and
threats alone is of minimal value to managers and decision
makers. From a SWOT analysis, four basic strategies can be
identified.
Opportunities Threats
Strengths Offensive Defensive
Weaknesses Reorientation Survival
Figure 44.2 - SWOT analysis and business strategies
Offensive strategies -The ideal situation occurs if a strength
meets an opportunity as this enables the business to gain
maximum benefit from a favourable external situation,
i.e., the business should make the most of the favourable
situation.
Defensive strategies -In this case, a strength meets an
external threat, so the situation presents an element of risk,
which requires the business to defend itself. Typically, this
strategy involves the business paying close attention to
the competition so that it does not lose market share (see
Chapter 23) or hinder its market dominance.
Reorientation strategies -In this case, there is a favourable
situation in the external environment, but which correlates
to an internal weakness. Hence, the business needs to
adjust or reorient its policies and practices. For example,
this strategy could involve the business trying to cut costs
to improve its liquidity position (see Chapter 18), remain
competitive and gain market share.
Survival strategies -The most undesirable situation occurs
if a weakness meets an external threat. Survival policies are
aimed at minimising the adverse effects of such a situation.
This means that the business has to pay maximum attention
to avoid a disastrous outcome and to survive.
Finally, it is important to remember that SWOT analysis does
not guarantee that a strategy will be successful. For example,
identifying weaknesses and threats does not necessarily mean
that the business has sufficient financial and human resources
to tackle these risks.
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Exam tip!

When using a SWOT analysis in the exam, do not present
the SWOT in tabular form. Using such a format can
encourage you to squeeze your answers to fit inside
a table that you have drawn. Examiners prefer written
explanations and justifications. It is acceptable to write
in bullet point format under each SWOT heading so long
as the examiner can understand the reasoning behind
your arguments.
Exam tip!

A common exam question will require you to examine the
current position of a business by using a SWOT analysis
framework. Therefore, be sure to learn how to use a SWOT
analysis properly. Remember that the strengths and
weaknesses refer to the current and internal position of
the organization. The opportunities and threats should
stem from a STEEPLE analysis of the external environment
(see Chapter 46, Business Management Toolkit 3).
Evaluation of SWOT analysis

SWOT analyses often lack quantitative assessment, with no
value for the costs of addressing an identified weakness or
potential rewards from pursuing an identified opportunity.
Unlike some other tools, such as decision trees and force field
analysis (see Chapters 49 and 55 respectively), the use of SWOT
analysis does not prioritise issues for managers and decision
makers.
Typically, SWOT analysis cannot be used in isolation. After all,
a SWOT analysis only assesses the current situation and does
not suggest any actual strategy. Better decisions are made if
more information is available, so other tools may be required
to achieve this. Nevertheless, as it encourages managers to
think holistically and collaboratively, SWOT analysis can help
to reduce the overall risks of decision-making by demanding
objective, more informed and logical thought processes.

and simple, allowing managers to organize their thinking and KEY TERMS

However, SWOT analysis can be overly simplistic and does not

The Ansoff matrix

The Ansoff matrix

The Business Management toolkit is a set of
situational, planning and decision-making tools used
to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content as well
as being applied in different contexts. The Ansoff
matrix is a decision-making tool. Chapter references have been
included as suggestions to show where the Ansoff matrix can be
applied in various parts of the syllabus.
© IBO, 2022
T

he Ansoff matrix (1957) is an analytical tool that helps
managers to choose and devise various product and
market growth strategies. Professor Igor Ansoff (1918
showed the different growth strategies that a firm can
take depending on whether it wants to sell new or existing
products in either new or existing markets (see Figure 45.1).
The four product-market growth strategies or growth options,
in this model are explained below.
Products

Figure 45.1 - The Ansoff Matrix
(i) Market penetration

Market penetration is the growth strategy that involves a
business choosing to focus on selling existing products in
existing markets, i.e., to increase their market share of current
products. Hence, this is a relatively low-risk growth strategy.
Market penetration might be achieved by offering more
competitive prices (see Chapter 28) or by improved advertising
(see Chapter 29) to enhance the desirability of the product. In
addition to attracting more customers, firms might attempt to
entice existing customers to buy more frequently, perhaps by
offering customer loyalty schemes (see Chapter 43). Brands
might also be repositioned (see Chapter 24) to achieve market
penetration.
An advantage of market penetration is that the business focuses
on markets and products that it is familiar with. Hence, market
research expenditure (see Chapter 26) can be minimised. It is
also the safest of the four growth strategies.
A limitation of market penetration is that competitors,
especially stronger rivals, are likely to retaliate to any business
trying to take away their customers and market share. This can
lead to aggressive reactions, such as price wars (see Chapter
28), thereby harming profits in the short term at least. Also,
once existing markets become saturated, alternative growth
strategies are required if the business is to continue its growth
and evolution.
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

{ii} Product development
Product development is a growth strategy that involves selling
new products in existing markets. Hence, this strategy carries
a medium level of risk for the business. Apple's launch of the
iPhone in 2007 revolutionised the mobile phone industry and
propelled the profits for the computer manufacturer founded
in 1976. McDonald's often adds new products to its menu.
Car manufacturers introduce new models and occasionally
limited editions of their cars. These are all examples of product
development growth strategies.

Figure 45.2 - McDonald's product development strategy
involves new additions to its menu
Product development tends to rely heavily on product
extension strategies to prolong the demand for goods and
services that have reached the saturation or decline stage of
their product life cycle (see Chapter 27). Product development
is also reliant on brand development to appeal to the existing
market. For example, well-established companies such as Sony
or Nike can use their brand names to launch new products to
the market as there are fewer risks of introducing a new product
under a well-known and trusted brand.

Product development is also a reason for mergers and

{iii} Market development
Market development is the growth strategy that involves selling
existing products in new markets, i.e., an established product is
marketed to a new set of customers. This might be done through
new distribution channels such as selling the existing product
overseas (although this could be quite risky if the business
is unfamiliar with local market conditions and cultures).
Alternatively, promotional strategies could be tweaked to
make the product more appealing to the new audience. Pricing
methods (see Chapter 28) could also be changed to attract
different market segments.
A key advantage of this growth strategy is that the business
is familiar with the product that is being marketed. For
example, Nike and Adidas successfully market their clothing
products for leisure rather than specifically for sports. Nokia
uses market development to sell its excess supply of mass-
produced smartphones that have a short product life cycle in
more economically developed countries (where customers
frequently upgrade their devices) by selling these in lower
income countries such as Sri Lanka, Indonesia and Nigeria.
However, the success of a product in one market does not
necessarily guarantee its success in other markets. Market
development is a medium risk growth strategy as it involves
the business competing in new markets. For example, French
retailing giant Carrefour pulled out of Thailand, Malaysia
and Singapore in late 2010 after failing to establish a market
presence. American retail giant Target closed more than 130
stores in Canada in 2015 for similar reasons, citing cultural
differences (see Chapter 11). Google struggled to establish itself
in China, where local company Baidu maintains around 85%
market share.
acquisitions with other companies (see Chapter 5). For example, {iv) Diversification
Tata Motor's acquisition ofJaguar Land Rover in 2008 meant it
could cater for different types of customers without the huge
costs and risks of starting a new company.

Case study 45.1 - Tata Motors
Tata Motors was founded in 1945 and has become India's
largest automaker, with a product range that includes
cars and sports utility vehicles, commercial vans, trucks,
buses, coaches and military vehicles. In 2004, it acquired
South Korean truck manufacturer Daewoo Commercial
Vehicles Company. In 2008, it purchased UK luxury
brands Jaguar and Land Rover. It also produced the Tata
Nano, once the world's cheapest mass-produced car.
Diversification is a high-risk growth strategy that involves selling
new products in new markets. For example, the Virgin Group
is a diversified company with its various strategic business units
(see Case Study below). In addition to capturing market share
in established markets, a key driving force for diversification is
to spread risks by having a well-balanced product portfolio (see
Chapter 27). Diversification is also suitable for businesses that
have reached saturation and are seeking new opportunities for
growth.
One way to diversify is to become a holding company. This is
a business that owns (or holds) a controlling interest in other
diverse companies. This means the holding company owns
enough shares in other businesses to be able to take control.
Holding companies (or parent companies) can benefit from
having a presence in a variety of industries in different regions
of the world. An example is Warner Media, the parent company
of numerous subsidiaries (firms owned by a holding company)
including Warner Bros, Cinemax, DC Comics, CNN, HBO and
Cartoon Network.

Case study 45.2 - Virgin Group

Virgin Group Ltd. is a UK multinational conglomerate,
co-founded by Sir Richard Branson and Nik Powell
in 1970. The company is a truly diversified business,
with operations in industries as diverse as healthcare,
travel, media, entertainment, hospitality, retail,
telecommunications, banking, motorsport, cruise line,
charity and even aerospace.
There are two categories of diversification.

Related diversification occurs when a business caters
for new customers within the broader confines of the
same industry. For example, many large commercial

fragrance industry in the 1990s which caused much offense to
its loyal customer base. Next, the UK clothing retailer, failed
to establish itself in the tablet computers market in 2010. The
Virgin Group tried to take on Coca-Cola and Pepsi by launching
Virgin Cola, but only managed to capture a market share of 3%
in the UK.

Related diversification is less risky as it builds on the

Evaluation of Ansoff's matrix

The Ansoff matrix is a decision-making tool that provides a
simple way for managers and entrepreneurs to compartmentalise
various growth strategies based on a business providing
existing or new products in new or existing markets. The tool
prompts discussions about the potential risks and rewards of
each potential growth strategy.

market development strategy is likely to require decision makers
to investigate the challenges of entering new markets, especially
those in overseas locations. Decision makers are also likely
to conduct a competitor analysis to determine the probable
reactions of existing firms in the market. This also applies to a
diversification growth strategy as it carries even more risk. This
means the Ansoff Matrix may be used alongside other Business
Management tools, such as SWOT and STEEPLE analyses
(see Chapters 44 and 46 respectively), in order to gain a more
complete picture and to make better-informed decisions.
However, the tool does not quantify these risks and rewards
(unlike decision trees, for example) nor does it actually suggest
a particular strategy that the business should pursue (unlike
forcefield analysis, for example). In reality, firms are not limited to a single growth strategy. Large
multinational companies competing in highly contestable

REVIEW QUESTIONS
What is the Ansoff matrix?
Why is market penetration a relatively low-risk growth
strategy?
Why is product development a medium-risk growth
strategy?
Why is market development also a medium-risk growth
strategy?
What makes diversification the highest risk growth strategy
in Ansoff's matrix?
KEY TERMS
The Ansoff matrix (1957) is a decision-making tool used to
devise various product and market growth strategies, depending
on whether businesses want to market new or existing products
in either new or existing markets.

Diversification is a growth strategy in the Ansoff matrix,
which involves an organization launching new products in new
markets.

A holding company (or parent company) is a diversified
business that owns a controlling interest in other diverse
companies.

Market development is a growth strategy in the Ansoff matrix
that focuses on using customer loyalty to persuade current and
prospective customers to purchase a new product from the
business.

Market penetration is a growth strategy in the Ansoff matrix
that focuses on developing existing markets with existing
products, in order to increase the firm's sales revenue and
market share.

Product development is a growth strategy in the Ansoff matrix
that involves introducing new products to existing customers
by developing or replacing current products.

STEEPLE analysis
''The reasonable man adapts himself to the world; the unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to himself."
George Bernard Shaw (1856 - 1950), Irish author
STEEPLE analysis

The Business Management toolkit is a set of
situational, planning and decision-making tools
used to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content as
well as being applied in different contexts. STEEPLE
analysis is a situation tool.
© 180, 2022
S

TEEPLE is an acronym for the Social, Technological,
Economic, Environmental, Political, Legal and Ethical
opportunities and threats in the external business
environment. These factors, unlike internal ones, affect
all businesses yet are beyond the control of any individual
organization. STEEPLE analysis is a situation tool that is central
to formulating business strategy, such as assessing the feasibility
of an overseas investment project.

External factors that represent prospects for businesses are
called opportunities, such as lower tax rates and lower interest
rates. External factors that can harm a business are called
threats, such as a recession, oil crisis or major road works.

Figure 46.1 - Roadworks are a major external constraint
on local businesses

worked example on the following page, which explores some
of the opportunities and threats of multinational companies
operating in India.

Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Worked example - STEEPLE analysis of multinational companies operating in India
Social factors
Potential market of over 1.38 billion people (the second most populous country in the world)
A large and well-educated English-speaking workforce of around 130 million people.
Large yet increasing discrepancies in the distribution of income and wealth.
Language barriers in rural cities, with potential clash of national cultures in a multilingual and multi-ethnic country.
Technological factors
Growing number of technologically aware population (huge opportunities for firms providing products such as mobile
phones, personal computers, and Internet services). Bengaluru, the IT capital of India, is widely regarded as the "Silicon
Valley of India''.
Major industries include communications technology, biotechnology, computer software, automobiles, petrochemicals,
and pharmaceuticals.
Technologies are easily copied due to a lack of appropriate legislation.
Economic factors
Huge growth potential in financial markets.
Significant economic growth and rising disposable incomes (spending power) in India.
Improved infrastructure and market opportunities in cities such as Mumbai, Bengaluru, and New Delhi.
Relatively low costs of production (average wage rates are still very low).
Most people are employed in the agricultural sector, with India being one of the world's top producers of cereals (wheat,
rice and sugar), meat, fruits, vegetables, tea, coffee, cotton, coal and wool.
Infrastructure and economic stability are less attractive than in other countries such as China and the United Arab
Emirates.
The vast majority of the Indian population is still very poor, with a real GDP per capital of less than $2,000 in 2022.
Environmental factors
Major challenges for India include tackling air pollution, water pollution, littering, waste disposal and environmental
degradation.
The Indian government is taking a more proactive approach to enforcing environmental protection.
Political factors
Political reform in India will encourage better trade relations with other nations.
Legislation is less stringent than in other nations, thus placing fewer constraints on business activity.
Regarded as less politically stable and relatively corrupt compared with other countries in the region.
Poor enforcement of patents and copyrights might discourage technology transfer to India.
Legal factors
Strict compliance laws for foreign bank accounts and heavy penalties for tax evasion.
Employment legislation is often overlooked, such as poaching of staff from competitors is commonplace.
There are no specific data protection laws enforced in India.
Ethical factors
Corruption is widespread, which does little to help combat poverty and can harm India's international competitiveness.
Slow business negotiations because establishing a trusting relationship is a prerequisite to doing business in India.
Indian culture is averse to critical disagreements, such as saying 'no; as this is seen as being rather rude; disagreements
should be expressed in an ethical way, using diplomatic language.
It can be difficult for foreign businesses to penetrate the Indian economy without partnering with a local Indian company.
The importance of each opportunity and threat identified in a
STEEPLE analysis can be weighted in a scientific or objective
way. This is useful when trying to examine the advantages and
disadvantages of a decision. If the overall importance placed
on the opportunities of a decision outweigh the threats, then
the business is likely to pursue that option. However, in reality,
external factors are subject to rapid and unforeseeable change.
An external shock, such as a global pandemic or a financial
crisis, can jeopardize the chances of success despite what a
STEEPLE analysis initially revealed.

A key advantage of STEEPLE analysis is that it is relatively
simple to use. The analysis helps managers to be thorough
and logical in their analysis of the external opportunities and
threats faced by the business. It is also a useful situational tool
for brainstorming and discussions. STEEPLE analysis promotes
proactive and forward thinking, rather than static views based
on gut feelings. Hence, it is more likely that managers will
be better informed and prepared to deal with changes in the
external environment.

Exam tip!
It is not always necessary to conduct a full STEEPLE
analysis. In the real corporate world, managers may prefer
to use a PEST analysis, where political factors include
(where appropriate) legal opportunities and threats,
and social factors include ethical and environmental
opportunities and threats.

Social opportunities and threats
{STEEPLE analysis)
Social factors in a STEEPLE analysis can directly affect the
activities of a business. The values and attitudes of society
towards a wide range of different issues (such as business
ethics, social welfare, women, religion or animal rights) can
present both opportunities and threats for businesses. Social
factors include consideration of cultural and demographic
opportunities and threats. Examples include the following:
The growing public support for environmental protection
has altered business behaviour, with many organizations
now reporting non-financial aspects of their operations,
such as recycling and waste management.
With a more liberal and modern social attitude towards
women in most societies, businesses have benefited from
having a more flexible labour force.

Societal pressures for businesses to act more ethically and

Technological opportunities and

threats (STEEPLE analysis)

The technological environment refers to scientific knowledge
and application to the external environment that presents
constant threats and opportunities. Advances in technology
and work processes have improved productivity. For example,
Internet technologies (see Table 46.1) create countless
opportunities for entrepreneurs to set up and run their
businesses without some of the financial risks of establishing
a physical business. Success stories include Mark Zuckerberg
(Facebook), Kevin Systrom (Instagram), Reed Hastings and
Marc Randolph (Netflix), Zhang Yiming (Tik Tok) and Eric
Yuan (Zoom).

However, the high cost of staying up to date with technological
progress can cause problems for businesses. For example,
Airbus faced lengthy delays in the production of the A380
(the world's largest commercial aircraft) and subsequently had
to compensate its customers such as Emirates Airlines and
Singapore Airlines.

Technology affects all aspects of business functions. For
instance, the Internet has directly affected Human Resource
Management (in the recruitment process), Marketing (such as
e-commerce), Finance (annual reports are published online)
and Operations Management (such as access to benchmarking
data).

BMT 3 - STEEPLE analysis

Apart from the Internet, other opportunities that technology
can bring to businesses include:
New working practices - Many more businesses are
using flexible working practices (see Chapter 7), such as
enabling people to work from home, by using Information
Communication Technology (ICT). Global businesses are
also increasingly using video conferencing to cut the costs
of face-to-face meetings and international recruitment.
Marketing activities have also been affected, such as the
growing popularity of online advertising.
Increased productivity and efficiency gains -Robots and
machines are much faster yet more accurate than humans,
especially in the mass production of products over
prolonged periods of time. Unlike humans, machinery
can be made to work for very long hours without the need
for breaks, financial rewards, motivation or maternity
leave! Firms are also more likely to achieve zero defects
(no wastage) from the use of technology (see Chapter 40).
Automated stock control systems can automatically re-
order stocks. Despite the large initial costs of automation
and technology, capital-intensive firms can benefit from
cost savings in the long run.
Quicker product development times -The use of CAD/CAM
technology (computer aided design and computer aided
manufacturing) has allowed firms to produce prototypes
in a timely and cost-effective way, thereby accelerating the
design, manufacturing and launch of new products.
Table 46.1 - Opportunities and threats of internet technologies

Opportunities
Speed of access to information -Businesses and customers can
gain access to up-to-date information from any part of the
world through dedicated websites, such as the huge range of
online news media sources that give invaluable information to
users in a cost-effective way.
Reducing language and cultural barriers -Information on the
Internet can be easily translated into different languages by
using dedicated software or translators. This can also help to
reduce the costs of trading overseas.
Reduced costs -Firms with an online presence can benefit
immensely from e-commerce. Trading can take place at any
time from any part of the world without the need for a physical
outlet. Therefore, labour costs can also be reduced.
Overcoming geographical limitations -The Internet makes
location less of an issue for many businesses. The increasing
use of mobile devices has fuelled e-commerce and literally
eliminated any limitations of geographical proximity to physical
retailers.
Threats
Price transparency - Firms are exposed to the forces of
competition as customers can easily compare the prices of
different businesses without leaving their home or office. In
addition, as there is no physical presence, it can be difficult to
judge a product's quality relative to the price.
Online crime -Hackers have cost e-commerce businesses a
huge amount of money. Online banking scams and credit card
fraud are quite common. This threat has therefore restricted the
number of online customers.
Higher production costs -In addition to the costs of online crime,
businesses also face maintenance and training costs to ensure
that employees are competent and confident in their use of the
latest Internet and online technologies.
Reduced productivity -Surveys from around the world have
consistently shown that labour productivity is harmed by
employees who regularly access personal emails and social
media websites during working hours.
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Job creation -Advances in technology bring about a need
for maintenance and technical support staff. Examples
include programmers, hardware and software engineers,
graphic designers and ICT teachers/instructors.
New products and new markets -Technology is a source
of innovation and brings about new products in the
marketplace, such as wireless broadband services,
smartphones, high-definition 3D smart televisions, social
media platforms and electric vehicles. Apple's highly
successful range of innovative products elevated the
company to become one of the most valuable businesses
on the planet.
Figure 46.4-Electric cars are becoming increasingly
popular around the world
The technological environment also presents certain threats to
businesses, such as:

Technology is not always reliable or secure -Computer failure
or hacked files can present serious problems for businesses.
For example, in December 2013, over 40 million credit and
debit card records were hacked from US retailer Target. In
2018, Facebook was in trouble with the law due to a massive
data scandal, with allegations of misuse of personal data to
influence the 2016 US presidential elections and the Brexit
vote (the UK leaving the European Union).
Shorter product life cycles (see Chapter 27) - Equipment and
software may become obsolete increasingly quicker and
therefore need to be upgraded regularly. This can make it
gradually more difficult for smaller firms to compete.
It can be costly-As products such as smartphones, flat screen
televisions and other electronic appliances have shorter life
cycles, businesses need to devote more resources to new
product development.
Job losses -Automation has led to unemployment in the
primary and secondary sectors, such as commercial
farming, oil extraction and car manufacturing. In the
tertiary sector, many supermarket checkout assistants
have been replaced with self-service checkout machines.
Therefore, businesses need to carefully manage the process
of staff redundancies (job losses).
Case study46.2-Tesco
In June 2010, Tesco opened the UK's first supermarket
without any checkout staff. Instead, one person is
hired at the store in Northampton to supervise the five
checkouts, mainly to assist customers who have not used
a self-service checkout before. Tesco, the UK's largest
retailer with over 28% market share in the groceries
industry, employs over 423,000 but critics argue that
such technologies would cause mass job losses. Today,
self-checkout tills are commonplace in retailing sector.
When adopting certain technologies, managers need to
consider several factors:
Costs - such as the cost of purchase, installation,
maintenance, depreciation, replacement ( upgrading) and
insurance of the new technologies.
Benefits - such as the expected gains in efficiency (as
measured by improvements in productivity, flexibility and
communications) and profits.
Human relations -such as the impact of resistance to change
and the impacts on morale, flexible working patterns and
workforce planning (see Chapter 7).
Recruitment and training -such as the costs of training
workers (see Chapter 7) to adopt the new technologies, the
number of people who need training and where to find the
time to train people.

to sell its 100 millionth console by the end of 2013. Its most popular game, Wii Sports, has sold over 83 million copies
worldwide by 2021. The Wii was replaced by the Wii U in November 2012 (the Xbox One and PlayStation 4 were not
released until November 2013). According to Nintendo, the company sold 425,000 unit of its Wii U in the first month of

Economic opportunities and

threats (STEEPLE analysis)

The economic environment refers to the state of the economy
in which businesses operate. This is determined by the
government's ability to achieve its key economic objectives: (i)
to control inflation, (ii) to reduce unemployment, (iii) to achieve
economic growth and (iv) to achieve a healthy international
trade balance. Government policies used to achieve these
fundamental goals will therefore present opportunities and
threats for businesses.

(i} To control inflation
Inflation is the continual rise in the general level of prices in
an economy. Most economists regard low and stable inflation
as a prerequisite to achieving the other three key economic
objectives, so this is an absolute priority for economic
prosperity. Inflation, if not controlled, can complicate business
planning and decision-making. For example, raw material
costs, catalogue and menu prices and wage claims are all
affected by inflation. Essentially, inflation that is not controlled
becomes a threat to businesses due to the higher costs and the
uncertainties that are caused.
