Evaluation of Gantt charts

Advantages of Gantt charts

Use of the tool enables project managers to monitor progress
oflarge projects in an efficient way. Gantt charts provide an
overall of a project and its timeline, enabling managers to
appropriate finance and resources appropriately for each
task.
They make complex information more manageable,
especially as a Gantt chart is presented as a visual planning
tool. This helps to simplify a complex set of tasks within a
large project. This helps team members to remain focused
BMT 9 - Gantt charts

As it is not easy to see dependencies in a Gantt chart, nor
is it possible to determine float times ( unlike with critical
path analysis), project managers cannot determine the
impact of a delay in the completion of an activity on the
overall completion of the project.
For large projects, with many different activities and tasks
that require a significant amount of time to complete,
it is not possible to display all the information on one
computer screen or a single sheet of paper. This can make
the information more challenging for project managers to
analyse.
and to avoid being overwhelmed by the large number of • In reality, not everything will necessarily go according to
tasks in the project. the plan in a Gantt chart. There may be unexpected delays
They improve efficiency by avoiding overlapping tasks
and showing dependencies. A Gantt chart clearly shows
how the beginning of one task can be dependent on the
completion of other preceding tasks. That allows project
managers to schedule tasks appropriately and to provide
the right resources for each task to ensure it completes on
time.
They enable managers to set realistic deadlines and
expectations of their teams. A Gantt chart illustrates all the
tasks that must be accomplished in order to realistically
complete a project on time. Consequently, having access
to such information allows managers to set realistic
or obstacles that arise, such as severe adverse weather
conditions or cases of major staff absences. Therefore, to
be of real value, Gantt charts may need to be regularly
updated.
As with all quantitative tools, the value of Gantt charts
depends on the accuracy of the underlying data. Project
managers need to have accurately identified all the relevant
activities in a project as well as their durations. For
substantial and multifaceted projects for which the business
lacks experience, it is likely that errors and omissions will
occur, thereby devaluing the predictions made in the Gantt
chart.

They can be motivational as team members can visualize

motivating them to complete their work on time so as to
not delay the project. Team members can see the progress
they contribute to the overall project, creating a sense of
value to the organization.

Porter's generic strategies (HL only)
"The essence of strategy is choosing what not to do."
Michael E. Porter (b.1947), American business strategy academic
Porter's generic strategies {HL

only)

The Business Management toolkit is a set of
situational, planning and decision-making tools
used to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content as
well as being applied in different contexts. Porter's
generic strategies is a type of decision-making tool.
© IBO, 2022
Professor Michael E. Porter's generic strategies is a business
management decision-making tool that outlines the ways
that any business can use to gain a competitive advantage. A
competitive advantage is any positive attribute or trait that
sets a business apart from its competitors, which enables it to
outperform its rivals.

If a profitable product or idea can be copied easily, then other
firms will take advantage by entering the market. Competitors
might offer an improved product or charge more competitive
prices, for example. Hence, the original firm would lose its
competitive advantage. Porter argued that every successful
business must have a competitive advantage in order to prevent
profits being eroded by rivals entering the market. He suggested
that there are three general or broad strategies that any business
can use to sustain a competitive advantage (see Figure 53.1).

Competitive advantage

Figure 53.1 -Porter's generic strategies
Cost leadership
Cost leadership is the generic strategy that involves a business
becoming the lowest-cost organization in the industry. Firms
using a cost leadership strategy strive to become the lowest cost
supplier of a product within market. For example, Malaysia's
AirAsia is the largest low-cost airline carrier in Asia (also
see Box 53.1). Aldi and Lid! are Germany's largest chains of
discount supermarkets that operate on an international scale.
IKEA, McDonald's, Netflix and Walmart also use this generic
strategy.
Note that although these firms are cost leaders, this does not
necessarily mean they charge the lowest prices in the market
(which is a different strategy known as price leadership).
However, cost leadership typically entails firms charging
L.___--

Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

low prices, but also allows them to be highly profitable and
market leaders in their respective industries. Cost leaders do
not compete with firms that offer higher-quality products
since this would require costs to increase. Alternatively, firms
might choose to use technology to cut wastage and to improve
productivity, thereby further reducing average costs.
There are two cost leadership strategies in Porter's generic
strategies model: cost leadership with parity and cost leadership
with proximity.

Cost leadership with parity (or cost parity) means charging
the same price as competitors for the same or similar good
or service but lowering costs, thereby increasing its profit
margin.
Cost leadership with proximity (or cost proximity) means
charging a lower price than the average competitor whilst
reducing costs which gives the business a price advantage
but often with a smaller profit margin.

Note that with both cost leadership strategies, if the business
can reduce its costs even further, it may be possible to reduce
price yet still earn the same or higher profit margins.
However, cost leadership (with parity or with proximity) can be
a risky strategy if more than one organization tries to achieve
competitive advantages in the same market by using the same
strategy. This will lead to a price war, which is usually disastrous
for businesses in the industry.
Exam tip!

Cost leadership is concerned with minimising costs of
production - this does not necessarily mean that prices
will be lower as the business can enjoy greater profit
margins. Remember that 'cost' (incurred by a business)
and 'price' (paid by customers) are separate concepts.
BMT 53 - Porter's generic strategies (HL only)

Differentiation
Differentiation happens when a firm makes its goods and
services distinct from those of its competitors in a way that
appeals to its customers (see Box 53.2). Unlike cost leadership,
differentiation focuses on the quality rather than the cost of a
product. It is about establishing a unique or distinctive selling
point for the business or its products. Apple, BMW, Chanel,
Lego, Nespresso, Nike, Rolex and Rolls-Royce all use this
strategy to maintain their competitive advantage.

A successful differentiation strategy will allow a business to
charge a premium price (see Chapter 28), which over and
above the cost incurred by differentiation and higher than the
industry average. This enables the business to earn a higher
profit margin.

Box 53.2 - Examples of differentiation
Branding
Colour
Customer service
Delivery options
Design
Exclusivity
Features and functions
Packaging
Quality (reliability, durability and performance)
Size
Technologies and innovations
Advantages of a differentiation strategy include:

A differentiation strategy allows businesses to make their
products more attractive to customers as these are distinct
from what competitors offer.
Product differentiation enables a business to charge
premium prices, enabling it to earn higher profit margins.
It encourages businesses to be more attentive and responsive
to the needs and desires of their customers.
A successful differentiation strategy encourages customer
loyalty and brand loyalty.
It can reduce the degree of rivalry within the industry,
thereby benefiting market leaders in particular.
It can also reduce the price elasticity of demand for products
(see Chapter 28) so that customers are less responsive or
less sensitive to changes in price.
Disadvantages of a differentiation strategy include:
Product differentiation is usually expensive, so will
increase costs of production, such as the amount of money
needed for research and development (see Chapter 42)
and to successfully promote and launch a product (see
Chapter 29). Although a premium price might be charged,
the business needs to ensure that the additional costs do
not exceed the price differential due to the differentiation
strategy.
A differentiation strategy requires businesses to continually
be innovative and creative in order to add value for
customers. This is both time consuming and draining of
the firm's scarce resources.
The strategy also requires substantial and sustained
marketing investment in order to attract a sufficient
number of customers.
Nevertheless, building a successful differentiation strategy can
give businesses, such as Amazon, Heinz and Omega, long-term
competitive advantages. They might choose to safeguard their
competitive advantage by using intellectual property protection,
such as copyrights, patents and trademarks (see Chapter 42).
Focus strategy
The third of Michael Porter's generic strategies is called focus,
which involves businesses concentrating on a narrow or niche
market. A focus strategy occurs when a business targets a
niche or single segment of the market. For example, IBID Press
focuses on providing specialized and high-quality textbooks
for 1B Diploma students. There are two alternatives to a focus
strategy:
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Cost focus -Businesses can gain a competitive advantage
by focusing on being a low-cost producer in narrow (niche)
markets. Examples include Claire's, an American retailer
of accessories and low-cost jewellery primarily aimed
at tweens and teen girls and Smart cars, which produces
microcars and subcompact cars. This strategy involves
businesses developing uniquely low-cost products for the
market.
Differentiation focus - Businesses can also gain a
competitive advantage by focusing on a particular market
segment. Examples include Rolls Royce, Rolex, Gucci and
Chanel. This strategy involves businesses developing well-
specified and high-end products for the market.
Focus can be a highly profitable strategy due to the high prices
that can be charged and the lack of competition in the market.
Businesses that adopt a focused strategy tend to build strong
brand loyalty amongst their customers. The main drawback is
that the market size is rather limited.

In summary, a cost focus strategy means a business concentrates
on cost-minimization within a narrow or niche market. A
differentiation focus strategy means a business concentrates on
strategic differentiation within a narrow or niche market.

Stuck in the Middle
Porter's generic strategies help managers to concentrate on
a specific strategy that best serves their organizations. The
framework suggests that it is not possible in the long-term to
adopt a mixture of these generic strategies. For example, it is
not feasible to maintain high quality by using a cost leadership
strategy, i.e. firms cannot expect to be highly profitable and to
have a corporate reputation of outstanding quality by charging
low prices.
Porter suggests that firms without a clear business strategy are
stuck in the middle, with detrimental consequences. Such
businesses do not have any sustainable competitive advantages,
regardless of the industry in which they operate. Instead, the
cost leaders, the differentiators and the focusers will all be better
positioned to compete against those stuck in the middle. As
Margaret Thatcher (the UK's first female Prime Minister) said,
"Standing in the middle of the road is very dangerous; you get
knocked down by the traffic from both sides." Essentially, Porter
argues that each generic strategy is fundamentally different so
requires a different approach to gain a competitive advantage.

BMT 53 - Porter's generic strategies (HL only)

Evaluation of Porter's generic strategies
Porter's generic strategies provides a clear and succinct
framework for businesses to formulate their growth strategies
(see Chapter 5). The growth and evolution of businesses can be
pursued by the implementation of any one of Porter's generic
strategies, such as economies of scale which are required to
pursue a cost leadership strategy

The advantages of using Porter's generic strategies as a business
decision making tool includes:

Porter's generic strategies provides a business with a
straightforward framework to decide which of the strategic
options to pursue (that is, cost leadership or differentiation)
and whether to target the mass market or a narrow (niche)
market.
As a strategic framework, it provides choice and flexibility
for entrepreneurs and decision makers in an organization.
For example, the right business strategy will change over
time as internal and external environments change (see
Chapter 44 about SWOT analysis).
However, as with all business management tools, Porter's
generic strategies as a decision-making framework has its
limitations. These include:

Porter's strategic framework provides theoretical strategic
choices but in reality, the pursuit of these strategies is not
always practical. For example, a business cannot simply
become the lowest cost provider in the market as this
requires significant market power and a large customer
base in order to achieve the necessary economies of
scale. Similarly, a business might not be able to pursue a
differentiation strategy due to the risks and financial costs
that this would involve.
It suggests that businesses should only pursue a single
strategy in order to prevent being 'stuck in the middle'. It is
possible and not uncommon for large businesses to focus
on differentiating themselves by producing good quality
products while paying attention to cost efficiency.
The pursuit of a generic strategy does not guarantee
corporate success. For example, cost leadership does not
always lead to high profit margins, especially in highly
competitive markets where low prices become the norm.
Differentiation does not always lead to higher market share.
For instance, whilst Apple's iPhones are highly innovative
(given the company a unique selling point), Samsung is the
market leader with its significantly larger product range of
smartphones.
The generic strategies are not necessarily sustainable
business strategies. For example, competitors can imitate any
of these generic strategies and/or changes in technologies
and innovations can eliminate any competitive advantage
that the business currently holds.
Overall, asa popular decision-makingtoolin the corporate world,
Porter's generic strategies help managers and entrepreneurs
to concentrate on a specific strategy to gain competitive
advantages. He argued that every successful business must have
a clear and distinctive competitive advantage in order to remain
relevant in the marketplace. For example, businesses can gain a
competitive advantage by either focusing on being a low-cost
producer (cost focus) such as discount bric-a-brac stores or
by differentiation within a particular segment (differentiation
focus) such as Ferrari and Gucci. Porter's generic strategies has
stood the test of time and is still widely applicable to almost any
business in literally every industry.

Hofstede's cultural dimensions (HL only)

Marcus M. Garvey, (1887-1940), Jamaican entrepreneur and political leader
Hofstede's cultural dimensions {HL

only)

The Business Management toolkit is a set of
situational, planning and decision-making tools
used to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content as
well as being applied in different contexts. Hofstede's
model of cultural dimensions is a type of situational tool.
© IBO, 2022
G

eert Hendrik Hofstede (1928 - 2020) was a Dutch
social psychologist and expert in corporate culture.
Professor Hofstede studied the links between
international cultures and organizational cultures. According
to Hofstede culture can be as "the collective mental programming
of the human mind which distinguishes one group of people from
another". This is largely shaped by domestic cultural norms
and shapes human behaviour in society. Cultural norms are
the shared expectations, values and rules that guide behaviour
of people within a social group. These norms are passed down
from one generation to the next.

This does not mean that everyone in a particular society
behaves in the same way as there are significant differences
between individual human beings. However, it does suggest
that there may be considerable differences among individuals
in one country that are noticeably different when compared
with cultures in different countries. Such differences in outlook
can cause culture clashes within an organization (see Chapter
11).

Hofstede's research gives insight into how organizational
cultures may differ from one country to another. National culture
has a direct impact on organizational culture. For example,
Universal Studios Singapore opened its theme park in 2010 on
18th March at precisely 8:28 a.m. with 18 Chinese lions blazing
through the entrance. The number 8 is auspicious in Chinese
culture. It is important for organizations with operations in
overseas markets to consider the cultural differences that exist.
What works well in one culture or country does not necessarily
apply to others (also see Chapter 34).
Figure 54.1 -Universal Studios, Singapore
.________._

Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Hofstede's cultural dimensions was based on his research of
employees working at IBM International ( where he worked as
a management trainer and manager of personnel research). He
interviewed IBM employees in over 70 national subsidiaries to
see how cultures may differ around the world within the same
organization. The research included Hofstede taking a two-year
sabbatical from IBM in 1971 and having conducted around
117,000 surveys, he discovered that there were significant
differences between cultures within the same organization in
different parts of the world.
Hofstede's original work found five dimensions (types) of
culture. These cultural dimensions describe broad patterns of
differences between cultures:
Power distance
Power distance measures the extent to which there is a clear
cultural sense of rank and status in society, i.e. whether
subordinates (or citizens) expect and accept unequal
distribution of power within an organization (or country).
Whilst some people or societies are expected and allowed to
challenge the views of their superiors, in others they are simply
expected to 'do as they are told'. In such a society, people are
not encouraged to ever challenge the ideas put forward by their
managers. Large power distance countries include Malaysia,
the Philippines and Slovakia. By contrast, a low power distance
rating or index, as found in New Zealand and Scandinavian
countries, reflects the society's view that people should have
equal rights.
Hofstede found that a high power distance culture tends to have
centralised decision-making and exists in organizations with
Individualism versus Collectivism
This cultural dimension in Hofstede's model measures the
extent to which people feel they should care for themselves
(individualism) versus caring for or being cared for by the
family network and others in society (collectivism). It considers
the extent to which people feel it is their responsibility to look
after others or whether they feel that this is the responsibility
of the government. The USA, UK and Australia are often cited
as individualist societies whereas collectivism is important in
Chinese, Columbian, Venezuelan and Pakistani cultures.
In a corporate setting, individualistic cultures put emphasis on
the needs of the individual over the needs of the group as a
whole. By contrast, a collectivist culture stresses the importance
of cooperation and interests of the group over the needs of any
particular individual.
Figure 54.2 - Collectivism is part of Chinese culture
tall hierarchical structures (see Chapter 8). This can create a 3. Masculinity versus Femininity
sense of alienation between senior management and employees.
workers may feel isolated, disconnected and unappreciated
especially if they have minimal, if any, influence in the decision-
making process. By contrast, a low power distance culture tends
to be decentralized, with delegation and empowerment (see
Chapter 10).
Differences in the power distance dimension of culture
mean that people will think and behave in different ways.
Understanding such differences and working to close the power
distance gap can help to prevent culture clashes (see Chapter
11) and make it less difficult for people from dissimilar regions
or cultures to work together effectively.
This cultural dimension focuses on the extent to which a culture
conforms to traditional gender values and traits. Masculinity
refers to the values and behaviours usually dominated by
males, such as assertiveness, competitiveness, ambition, status,
selfishness and material rewards. According to Hofstede Insights
(www.hofstede-insights.com), this culture is found in Japan,
Hungary and Slovakia for example. By contrast, femininity
refers to the values and attributes traditionally associated with
females, such as placing focus on relationships, cooperation,
communication and the general quality of life. This culture is
found in Thailand, Sweden, Norway and Latvia for example.
BMT 11 - Hofstede's cultural dimensions (HL only)

In the corporate world, a masculinity culture suggests preference
for achievement and material rewards as measures of success.
Such organizations do not emphasise harmony and consensus.
This differs from a femininity culture, such as observed in
charities and other non-profit social enterprises (see Chapter
2), which prefers cooperation, modesty, caring for the less able
and improving overall quality of life. Such organizations are
more consultative and consensus oriented.

Note that categorizing cultures as 'masculine' or 'feminine' was used by
Hofstede over 50 years ago, so the terms are less politically correct in
today's world - a clear example of how cultural and social norms change
over time!

Uncertainty avoidance
This aspect of Hofstede's cultural dimensions measures the
extent to which people in an organization or country prefer
structured routines (predictability) over flexible structures.
It refers to the extent to which individuals in society or
organizations are comfortable with uncertainty. Hofstede
found that countries with high uncertainty avoidance scores
have strong customs and habits. Examples include cultures
found in Greece, Portugal and Uruguay. Such societies tend
to favour formal structures, rules and regulations (see Chapter
8). In some organizations, people are used to receiving precise
instructions, with detailed to-do lists and plans. There are clear
guidelines and policies so that people know exactly what they
are expected to do and when. People who have a low tolerance of
uncertainty avoidance tend to remain loyal to their employers.

By contrast, a society or organization that has a high tolerance for
uncertainty avoidance means that there is generally acceptance
for new ideas and the ideas of others. Members do not feel
uncomfortable with doubt (uncertainty) and are receptive of an
unstructured future. Some of the most tolerant nations, with a
low uncertainty avoidance score, include Sweden, Denmark and
Singapore. Such cultures are conducive to change, growth (see
Chapter 5) and innovations (see Chapter 42). Hofstede found
that organizations that have a high tolerance for uncertainty are
suited to operating in fast-paced industries that witness rapid
changes.

Long-term versus short-term orientation
This dimension of culture looks at the extent to which a particular
culture values making sacrifices today for the benefits to be
reaped in the future. According to Hofstede Insights, countries
and companies with a culture of long-term orientation, such
as India, China, Japan, South Korea and Thailand are focused
on the future so invest for the future, have perseverance and
are patient with the results. People in such cultures do not seek
instant gratification but willingly sacrifice current consumption
for future benefits.
Figure 54.3 - Long-term orientation does not seek instant
gratifications
By contrast, short-term orientation means that cultures and
traditions are kept because people are focused on the present
or past and consider this to be more important than the
future. They view societal change with an element of suspicion
and apprehension. Such orientation, as found in Columbia,
Trinidad and Tobago and numerous nations of West Africa,
involves people fulfilling their social obligations and respect
for and preservation of tradition. Hence, such cultures can be
resistant to change (see Chapter 7).
In the corporate world of business, these different outlooks
with respect to time directly impact on investment decisions
(see Chapter 21). Some managers may only look two or three
years ahead, expecting the business to reach break-even quickly
(see Chapter 39) and earn a high return on investment in that
time. However, other managers are willing to take longer term
decisions and risks. They are willing to persevere and work
harder for a longer time period to achieve success.
L...__---

Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Indulgence versus self-restraint
In 2010, Hofstede's research led him to add a sixth cultural
dimension: indulgence versus self-restraint. An indulgent
culture is one that enables people to let go, have freedom of
speech, enjoy life and have fun as a way of life, whereas a culture
that emphasises self-restraint has strict social norms to ensure
self-regulation and control.
Examples of indulgent countries, according to Hofstede
Insight, include Australia, Canada, the US, Argentina, Mexico,
El Salvador and Chile. Countries with a moderate level of
indulgence include Finland, Sweden, Turkey and Algeria.
Pakistan, India, China, Japan, Latvia and Estonia have a culture
of self-restraint. People from countries with low scores for
indulgence (or high ratings for self-restraint) may be reluctant
to offer their personal opinions and may feel guilty or a sense of
shame for engaging in trivial activities. They may also consider
those who openly indulge as being unprofessional.
As with all dimensions of culture, having an understanding of
cultural differences and local business etiquette improves the
chances of commercial success. It is therefore vital for managers
to be open-minded, mindful and flexible in international social
and business encounters.
Case study 54.3 -Culture and etiquette in China
Fresh fruits are often given as gifts in Chinese culture
The eldest person is always greeted first.
Business cards should be exchanged with both
hands but placing the business card straight into
your pocket is regarded as offensive behaviour.
Fruits and food items are generally appropriate gifts.
Gifts must be received with both hands - and should
not be opened in front of the benefactor.
It is not acceptable to use red ink for written
communications.
Clocks should never be given as a gift!
Male colleagues should refrain from wearing green
hats if they want any respect!

Evaluation of Hofstede's cultural
dimensions
Hofstede's cultural dimensions gives managers and decision
makers a coherent tool for classifying and discussing cultures
within and across organizations. The tool helps to explain a
range of social behaviours, based on empirical evidence. A major
strength of this tool is that it can help to prevent or minimize
culture clashes due to ignorance or misunderstandings,
especially in large and multinational companies (see Chapter
6). This helps managers to plan and adapt corporate strategy

Globalization has caused the corporate world to be more
integrated and interdependent. Numerous sub-cultures may
therefore exist in organizations. The trend towards hiring a
workforce that is culturally diverse means that managers and
employees may not make decisions in the same way as described
by Hofstede's original research and findings. Whilst his research
was comprehensive, it is somewhat outdated. For example,
describing cultural dimensions as 'masculine' or 'feminine' may
seem sexist or offensive in today's business world.
more appropriately. There are many factors that influence culture, not just national

Question 54.1 - Wahaha and Danone's joint venture
Wahaha, China's largest beverage producer, formed a joint venture with France's largest food company, Danone, in 1996.
When Wahaha's founder stepped down in 2007, several disputes broke out between the two companies, including the
choice of a new chairperson. Both companies wanted their own representative to take over the company. Danone then

Force field analysis

F

orce field analysis was developed by German American
social psychologist Kurt Lewin in 1943. It is a situational
and decision-making tool that deals with the forces
for and against change. Professor Lewin (1890 - 1947) argued
that successful businesses tend to be constantly adapting and
changing, rather than being fixed in outdated practices and
unable to look or move forward. Force field analysis consists of
two types of forces:

List the driving forces in favour of change and the
restraining forces against change.
Allocate a statistical weight to each of these forces, from 1
(weak) to 5 (strong) based on the level of importance to the
organization and then total the scores for the driving forces
and restraining forces.
Construct the FFA diagram for a visual representation of
Driving forces push for change. These represent the the results (see Figure 55.1).
arguments or reasons for change.
Analyse the results in order to (i) decide whether or not to
Restraining forces act against change. These are the factors proceed with the proposed change, (ii) determine how best
(or forces) that resist change. to weaken the restraining forces and (iii) decide how best
to strengthen the driving forces.
The relative strength of these forces determines whether the
change should take place (be implemented in the workplace). For example, a business deciding whether to transfer its
production facilities to an overseas location might produce a
There are several steps involved in a force field analysis (FFA): FFA that looks similar to the one in Figure 55.1:
Identify the goal (purpose of the proposed change).

Figure 55.1 - Example of a force field analysis
Figure 55.1 shows that in this case the driving forces for
change outweigh the restraining forces against the change.
Even if managers have already decided they prefer this option,
conducting a FFA can help to make this decision more objective.
It also provides a framework for managers to consider how best
to improve the project's chances of success. This is done by
investigating how the driving forces can be strengthened and
how the restraining forces can be minimized.

Whilst the problems of change management and resistance to
change (see Chapter 7) are not solved by FFA, it still enables
managers to examine the driving and restraining forces in a
more coherent and focused way. Lewin argued that progress is
not the result of one-off changes but by many small changes and
improvements.

The advantages of using FFA as a situational and decision-
making tool include:

It offers a visual interpretation of the driving forces for
and restraining forces against change. This makes it more
straightforward to understand the different factors that
need to be considered in order to make better informed
choices.
The statistical weights used in FFA help managers and
decision makers to look at business problems and issues
in a more logical and methodical way. This can improve
business decision making and help organizations to
develop more suitable business plans (see Chapter 48) to
achieve their organizational objectives (see Chapter 3).
Unlike SWOT analysis (see Chapter 44) or STEEPLE
analysis (see Chapter 46), the use of FFA analysis requires
managers and decision makers to assess the relative
strengths of the driving and restraining forces by applying
a statistical weight to each of these factors.
There are two main weaknesses of using FFA as a situational
and decision-making tool:
The weights attached to the driving and restraining forces
might be done subjectively rather than based on facts or
evidence, perhaps to over-emphasise the need for change.
Not all relevant forces might be considered. There is
always a possibility that some factors, be they driving and/
or restraining forces, can arise that were not previously
considered as managers did not think these actually existed
at the time.
Exam tip!
It is important to note that the quantity of driving forces
and restraining forces in a FFA is not as important as
the relative strength (weights) of each force. So, whilst
there could be many different restraining forces against a
certain option, simply one or two very important (heavily
weighted) driving forces may be sufficient to convince
decision makers to proceed with the proposed change.

in order to increase its output. The team has identified the following driving and restraining forces as well as attaching their
weights to each of these factors. These weights are the numbers shown in brackets (where 1 = weak and 5 = strong).

(b) Comment on the results of your force field analysis for TE. [2 marks]
Evaluation of force field analysis

Overall, the effectiveness of force field analysis will depend
on the quality of the data (in terms of suitability, breadth and
depth) and how well or accurate the data is interpreted in order
to select the right choice. Despite the tool relying on scientific
decision-making processes, the role of intuitive thinking and
management (see Chapter 9) can skew the results of a force field
analysis. Hence, the outcomes of a FFA can have a direct impact
on whether implementation of an organization's strategic plan
is effective in influencing change.

Possibilities

Possibility

Figure 55.2 - FFA can help managers to make more informed
decisions
Nevertheless, Lewin's force field analysis is a useful situational
tool as it allows managers to decide what might need changing
as well as looking at the forces acting for and against change.
It is also a useful decision-making tool as it informs managers
whether the restraining or driving forces are stronger. This
forms the basis for effective change management (see Chapter
7).
If change is desired, managers can analyse and devise appropriate
plans to influence the forces to make the change happen. FFA
is essentially a specialised technique of weighing up advantages
and disadvantages to help decide whether a proposed change
is worth implementing. Hence, FFA can be used as a strategy
for reducing the impact of change and resistance to change
(see Chapter 7). However, as the tool is static (representing
the position at one point in time, it is important for managers
to continually review the situation and progress because the
driving and/or restraining forces can change at any time due to
changes in the internal and external environments (see Chapter
46).
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Finally, it is important to note that for this tool to be of any
real value, force field analysis requires managers and decision
makers to apply the weights to each restraining and driving
force in an objective and honest manner. If the weights are
assigned arbitrarily, the results will add very little, if any, value
to the decision-making process.

Critical path analysis (HL only)
"The people may be made to follow a path of action, but they may not be made to understand it."
Confucius (551 BC - 479 BC), Chinese Philosopher
Critical path analysis (HL only)

The Business Management toolkit iis a set of
situational, planning and decision-making tools used
to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content as well
as being applied in different contexts. Critical path
analysis is a type of planning tool.
© IBO, 2022
Critical path analysis (CPA) is a management planning tool
which serves to improve the efficiency of the production
processes in a project. It does this by systematically scheduling
all tasks and resources required to complete a project in the
minimum amount of time. Critical path analysis ( or the critical
path method as it is often called) is an essential tool used in
project management. CPA was developed by fellow Americans
James E. Kelley and Morgan R. Walker in 1956.

Project management is the planning and coordination
of different jobs and tasks in a particular project. It is
especially important for firms dealing with large projects and
developments, such as the construction of motorways, bridges
and residential property. Such projects can involve the planning
and coordination of hundreds or even thousands of different
jobs and tasks. Some activities will take longer than others,
whilst some jobs must be completed before another task begins
and yet other activities can take place at the same time. CPA
stresses the importance of placing the various activities of a
project into a coherent sequence. This is particularly important
for complicated and large projects that need to be managed and
controlled carefully.

Figure 56.1 - Critical path analysis is a crucial part of project
management
Unit 5.6 Production planning (see Chapter 40) explained that
idle resources and stockpiling are costly to a business. There is
little point in buying stocks (inventories) and hiring labour in
advance when they are not to be used for several days, weeks
or even months. Critical path analysis (sometimes referred to
as network analysis) involves setting deadlines for all tasks
to ensure the smooth operation and progress of the project.
From the network analysis (presented as a diagrammatic
interpretation of the various sequences and tasks in the project)
project managers can attempt to minimise production costs
by allocating resources to complete the project in the shortest
available time.
Production delays can be very costly to a business. For example,
Airbus initially claimed it would reach break-even on its 'super
jumbo' Airbus A380 on the sale of 250 units. However, due
to major production problems and delays, Airbus announced
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

within a year of the initial statement that the revised break-
even figure had increased by 68% to 420 units (partly due to
financial compensations to airlines such as Singapore Airlines
and Emirates for late deliveries).

Critical path analysis diagrams

Completion and analyses of a critical path diagram (drawing of the
diagram is not expected).
© IBO, 2022
The ultimate purpose of critical path analysis is to identify the
minimum amount of time needed to complete a project. It
requires the various tasks of a project to be planned in a logical
and coherent way so that the different processes are completed
with minimal delay and maximum efficiency.

The process of network analysis (or critical path analysis)
involves the following steps:

Identifying all the operations required for the completion
of a project.
Breaking down the project into separate tasks.
Determining how long each task is expected to take.
Identifying all dependencies in the project (activities that
cannot start until the completion of other prior jobs).
Determining which tasks can take place concurrently (to
minimize production time).
Placing all operations in the right sequence on a network
diagram.
Node Earliest start

finishing
time (LFT)
Showing the earliest start time (EST) and the latest finishing
time (LFT) of each activity in the project.
Identifying the critical path from the network diagram
(the minimum time needed to complete the whole project).
Activities that cannot be delayed are known as critical activities.
Any hold-ups to these operations on the critical path will delay
completion of the project.
Constructing networks diagrams
There are several key features shown in a network analysis
diagram:
Nodes show the start and finish times of each activity
within the project (see Figure 56.2). Each node is numbered
to identify the sequence of activities.
4
Arrows are used to show the sequence and duration of each
activity or task in the project.
The earliest start time (EST) of each activity is shown in
the top right-hand part of the node (see Figure 56.2). This
shows when a particular activity can begin. The EST will
depend on the duration of all previous activities.
The latest finishing time (LFT) is the deadline for a
particular activity to be completed so that the entire
project can finish in minimal time. The LFT of each activity
is shown in the bottom right-hand part of the node (see
Figure 56.2).
The float shows the difference between the EST and LFT
for each activity. It identifies any spare time that might exist
for particular tasks.

The following can be seen from Figure 56.5 above:

Task A takes 7 days to complete. Therefore, the EST for

Task C starts on day 9 with a duration of 5 days. Hence, it is

Task E can only start when both tasks C and D are

Task E takes a further 3 days, so the shortest time the entire
project can be completed is 19 days.
BMT 13 - Critical path analysis (HL only)

The next step is to calculate the latest finishing time (LFT)
for each activity without extending (or delaying) the whole
project. In order to work out the EST, we work from left to
right. Conversely, to work out the LFT, we must work back
from right to left. In this case, we start at Node 5 as shown
in Figure 56.5. As the shortest time needed to complete
this project is nineteen days, then the LFT must also be 19
days if there is to be a critical path. The LFT for all previous
nodes is calculated by using the formula:
LFT = EST (next node) - Duration

So, for example, the LFT for activity A as shown in Figure 56.6
below is calculated as: 9 - 2 = 7.

The free and total float
Calculation of free float and total float.
© IBO, 2022
The float in a critical path analysis identifies any activities that
can be delayed without affecting the deadline of the project.
Calculating the float allows project managers to consider
how best to use any spare time, perhaps by coordinating staff
and resources more effectively. First, consider the following
sequence of events for Project X.

BMT 13 - Critical path analysis (HL only)

Hence, the critical path for Project Xis B, C, D, F and G. This is
shown in the network diagram by 'double striking' the activities
on the critical path.

The activities that are not on the critical path (in this case, tasks
A and E), have some spare or float time. This means that they
can be delayed without affecting the estimated completion
time of the overall project. In other words, trying to speed up
these activities does not get the project completed any sooner.
Calculating the float can be important as managers will become
aware of the maximum time that the activity can be delayed;
holdups that are longer than the float time will cause a delay
to the overall project. There are two main ways to calculate the
float: (i) the free float and (ii) the total float.

(i} The free float

The free float refers to the amount of time that an activity can
be delayed without affecting the EST of the next activity in the
project. Of course, activities on the critical path do not have any
float time. The formula for calculating the free float is:

Free float= EST of next node -Duration -EST of current node

For Project X, only two activities do not lie on the critical path,
namely activities A and E. Using the formula, the free float
for activity A is 5 - 1 - 0 = 4, as shown in Figure 56.10 below.
This means activity A can be delayed by up to 4 weeks without
delaying the EST of the next activity (in this case, activity D).

Figure 56.10 - Calculating the free float (Activity A)
The free float for activity E is 11 - 2 - 8 = 1 week. This means
that activity E can be completed by the 10th week but has a
float of 1 week as the following activity (in this case, activity
G) cannot start until week 11 when activity F has also been
completed.

(ii} The total float
The alternative approach to calculating the free float is to use the
total float. This refers to the amount of spare time available to
an activity without causing a delay to the overall (total) project.
The calculation of total float for each individual activity is found
by the formula:
Total Float= LFT -Duration -EST
So, for activity A ( which only takes 1 week to complete) the total
float is 5 - 1 - 0 = 4 weeks. This is because activity D cannot
start until activity C is completed, on week 5 at the earliest. For
activity E, the total float is 11 - 2 - 8 = 1 week, as shown in
Figure 56.11.

Dummy activities

A dummy activity ( or sometimes referred to as a dummy
variable) is a logical dependency between two indirectly linked
tasks. It is used to prevent an illogical path from being followed
in a network diagram and is shown by a dotted arrow line in a
network diagram (see Figure 56.13). As an example, consider
the following plan of events for Project Y:

Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Evaluation of critical path analysis

As a planning tool, critical path analysis can provide numerous
benefits for project management. These advantages include:

CPA provides a visual representation of a complex project
which can therefore make it easier for people to interpret.
As a planning tool, CPA encourages forward planning and
enables project managers to consider different aspects of
a particular project, such as the management of different
resources at different stages of the project.
It promotes operational efficiency by identifying the critical
path (the shortest time in which a project can be completed).
By calculating float times and determining tasks that can
be carried out simultaneously, project managers are able to
reduce any lost time between different activities, thereby
ensuring the project runs smoothly. Operational efficiency
also means that the customer will get timely delivery of
their order.
CPA can help a firm with its budgeting (see Chapter 22)
and to have better cash flow management (see Chapter
20). By identifying when activities can start and how long
tasks should last, project managers can have better cost
control. This is particular important for businesses such
as construction companies that have long working capital
cycles (see Chapters 19 and 20).
Similarly, CPA can be useful for production planning
and stock control (see Chapter 40). Raw materials and
components only need to be ordered in time for the EST
of each activity and no sooner. This also helps to reduce
storage costs.
CPA can be used for a range ofbusiness issues and problems,
from small-scale projects to huge undertakings that involve
thousands of processes. It works particularly well with just-
in-time production systems (see Chapter 37).
However, as with any quantitative tool, CPA also has its
limitations. These include:

No matter how impressive or well-planned, network analysis
does not guarantee that everything will go according to
plan. Internal and external factors (see Chapter 46) can
cause disruptions and delays to the completion of a project.
For example, poor weather can prolong construction
projects.
As with most quantitative tools, CPA is only useful if the
data used to construct the network analysis is accurate and
reliable.
The purpose of CPA is to determine the quickest time to
complete a given project. However, this does not guarantee
that the project is the best one to pursue. Other methods,
such as investment appraisal (see Chapter 21) can help to
determine whether the firm's resources could be used more
effectively on other projects.
Similarly, if any necessary steps are not identified in the
network analysis (perhaps due to oversight or a change
in unforeseen circumstances), then the CPA will be
inaccurate.
Constructing a CPA for huge-scale projects can be very
complex, highly challenging and time consuming. This
might make the process unmanageable (although there are
dedicated software packages that can help to tackle such
problems).
Nevertheless, in today's fast-paced and ever-competitive
business environment, business strategy calls for rapid product
development and the launch of new products to meet the
changing demands of consumers. This suggests that effective
use of CPA can provide businesses with a competitive edge as
they complete designated projects in a timely and cost-effective
way. As the example of the Airbus A380 has shown, production
delays can severely harm the financial position of a business.

Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

KEY TERMS

Critical activities are those along the critical path in a network
analysis. Any hold-ups to these operations will delay completion
of the project.
Critical path refers to the most efficient sequence of activities
which minimizes the overall time needed to complete a project.
This is shown in a network analysis diagram by double striking
('//') the critical activities.
Critical path analysis (CPA) is a project management planning
tool which serves to improve the efficiency of the production
process by systematically scheduling tasks and resources to
identify the least amount of time needed to complete a project.
Dependencies in a project are the activities that cannot start
until the completion of other prior tasks.
Dummy activity is a logical dependency between two indirectly
linked tasks in a project. It is used to prevent an illogical path
from being followed and is shown by a dotted line in a CPA
diagram.
Earliest start time (EST) shows when a particular activity can
begin, placed in the top right-hand part of a node. The EST
depends on the duration of all previous activities.
Float refers to the spare time (if any) that is available. Activities
that have float time can be delayed without affecting the
deadline of the project.
The free float refers to the amount of time that an activity can
be delayed without affecting the EST of the next activity in the
project.
Latest finishing time (LFT) is the deadline for a particular
activity so that the entire project can be completed in minimal
time. It is shown in the bottom right-hand part of a node.
Nodes show the earliest start times and latest finish times
of each activity within a project. Each node is numbered to
identify the sequence of activities in the project.
Project management is the planning and coordination
of different jobs and tasks for a particular project. It is
especially important when dealing with large assignments and
developments.
The total float refers to the amount of spare time available to an
activity without causing a delay to the overall project.

Contribution

The Business Management toolkit is a set of
situational, planning and decision-making tools used
to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content as well
as being applied in different contexts. Contribution
is a decision-making tool. The syllabus specifies three types of
contribution as part of the toolkit: (i) Make or buy analysis, (ii)
Contribution costing and (iii) Absorption costing.
© 180, 2022
C

ontribution refers to the difference between the sales
revenue earned from selling a product (its price) and
the variable costs of producing the product. Hence,
unit contribution is P - AVC, where P = price and AVC =
average variable cost (or the variable cost per unit).

A positive contribution exists when there is value added in
the production process (see Chapter 1). The financial surplus
(positive difference) is then used to 'contribute' to paying
towards the firm's fixed costs of production. Recall from Unit
3.3 (Chapter 16) that fixed costs are a firm's expenses that do
not change with the level of output, such as rent or interest
repayments on bank loans. By contrast, variable costs do change
with the level of output, such as the cost of raw materials.

For example, suppose a toy manufacturer has fixed costs of
$100,000, an average selling price of $5, variable cost per unit of
$2 and sale volume of 120,000 units. From this information, we
are able to determine the following:

Sales revenue = Price x Sales quantity = $5 x 120,000 =
$600,000
Total variable cost = Average variable cost x Quantity of
output= $2 x 120,000 = $240,000
Contribution per unit= Price - Average variable cost= $5
$2 = $3
Total contribution = Contribution per unit x Quantity of
output= $3 x 120,000 = $360,000
Profit = Total contribution - Fixed costs = $360,000 -
$100,000 = $260,000
Contribution analysis can be used as a decision-making
business management tool in several ways: (i) make or buy
analysis, (ii) contribution costing and (iii) absorption costing.
Make or buy analysis

A make or buy decision involves entrepreneurs and decision
makers determining whether to manufacture a product in-
house or to purchase it from an outsourced third-party supplier.
For example, none of the components of the iPhone are made
by Apple but outsourced to other companies such as Foxconn
and Pegatron, both of which are based in Taiwan.
As an example, suppose that a business can make a product for
$22 per unit or it can buy the same product from a supplier for
$24 each. Assume that this business has fixed costs of $4,000
per month. The make or buy decision can then be worked out
as follows:
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

The cost to buy (CTB) outweighs the cost to make (CTM)
by $2 per unit, i.e., CTM < CTB or $22 < $24.
However, the business still has fixed costs of $4,000 per
month.
This means that the business needs to sell at least 2,000
units per month to pay all of the fixed costs.
Therefore, so long as the business is able to cover all its
costs (fixed plus variable costs) per time period, it would
be financially sensible for this firm to make the product.
However, if sales forecasts are less than 2,000 units per
month, it is financially better for the firm to buy this
product from a supplier.
In general, if the CTM > the CTB, then it makes financial sense
for the business to buy the product from a third-party supplier.
The opposite is true if the cost to buy is greater than the firm's
cost to make, i.e., the business should manufacture the product
in-house). Please see Chapter 40 for more specific information
about the cost to make and the cost to buy.

The outcome of a make or buy analysis should be a rational
decision that maximizes the long-term financial benefits for
the business. Hence, knowledge of contribution analysis can
support a firm's internal and external growth strategies (see
Chapter 5). However, a make or buy decision is not necessarily
made on quantitative grounds.

Figure 57.1 - The make or buy decision is about making a
rational choice
Other factors that affect a make or buy decision include both
quantitative and qualitative reasons.

The timeframe in which the products can be produced
in-house compared with buying them from an external
vendor (seller). If urgent delivery to customers is required,
then the business is likely to choose the quickest option,
whereas if the order is not urgent the business may choose
the relatively cheaper option.
Spare capacity - Managers and decision makers will need
to consider whether the business has sufficient capacity
to produce the item in-house or whether it is cheaper and
more efficient to use an outsourced supplier.
Reputation and reliability of outsourced suppliers - The
make or buy decision will also depend on whether there is
a reliable supplier that can produce the product in sufficient
quantities, to the right quality specifications and completed
in a timely manner. It is essential the business can work
with an external supplier that they can rely on for the long-
term.
Expertise - The business needs to consider whether it
has sufficient expertise and know-how to make the item
in-house. Essentially, if the product can be made more
efficiently by an outsourced supplier, then it would make
financial sense to use a third-party provider.
Fixed costs - The business also needs to consider whether
it has funds to purchase the necessary equipment for
in-house production. This is a major concern for start-
up companies, which tend to lack finance and liquidity.
Established firms could think about whether outsourcing
the production could allow it to sell existing machinery
and equipment so the cash can be used elsewhere.
An assessment of the firm's core competencies and its
non-core activities and functions - For example, suppliers
might have specific areas of expertise and access to better
technological innovations.
Strategic importance - Managers and entrepreneurs will
need to decide whether the product is part of its core
competencies and key to its corporate strategy.
If the product is vital to the organization, it may convince
decision makers to manufacture the product in-house so
as to maintain complete control. Conversely, a product
that has less significance can more easily be passed onto an
outsourced supplier.
External influences - Factors in the external environment
can also have a direct impact on the make or buy decision
if an overseas supplier is involved. These factors include
the political climate, environmental considerations and
fluctuations in the exchange rate.
Contribution costing

Question 57.1 - Sarni Ikea Inc.

Sarni Ikea Inc. is a new business start-up. It can pay $30,000 for specialist machinery in order to have in-house production
at a variable cost of $5 per unit of output. Alternatively, Sarni Ikea Inc. can use an outsourced supplier that sells these
products for $10 each.
Using make or buy analysis, explain whether Sarni Ikea Inc. should produce the item in-house or purchase it from the
supplier. [4 marks]
Contribution costing is a method of valuing costs by allocating
direct costs to products or divisions (departments) of a business.
Indirect costs (or overhead costs) are not accounted for in this
method. For example, suppose a product has a selling price of
$8 and direct costs are $3 per unit. The contribution per unit
is therefore $5 (selling price minus unit variable costs). Hence,
each item sold enables the firm to contribute $5 towards paying
its fixed costs. If the fixed costs amount to $5,000 per month,
the firm makes a profit once it has sold more than 1,000 units
($5 x 100 units) each month.

Contribution costing also enables a business to set different
prices for different products in its portfolio, based on their level
of contribution. It can help a business to identify products
that are relatively profitable and ones that might need more
attention. Consider the data in Table 57.1 which shows how
contribution analysis might be used.

Examination of the below data suggests that all six products are
profitable because the unit contribution is positive. In general,
any product that makes a positive contribution is worth
considering as it helps towards payment of the firm's fixed
costs (and hence profits). Hence, the sale of each of the above
products contributes positively towards the fixed costs of Cafe
Cuppa. We can also see:

The strongest product is the Mocha; despite its relatively
high average cost of production, it earns the firm $3.40
contribution per unit sold.
The most vulnerable product is the Spring water which
only earns Cafe Cuppa $1 contribution per unit sold.
Table 57.1 - Contribution analysis for Cafe Cuppa

However, it is important to also know the number of
units sold before concluding which product is the most
profitable.
Nevertheless, it is clear that twice the number of units of
Orange juice needs to be sold in order to earn the same
contribution as one unit of Latte.
Note, as pointed out above, the indirect costs (or overhead
costs) of Cafe Cuppa are not accounted for in this method.

Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

Common mistake
Students who claim that a product should be
discontinued or reduced in price (to sell more) because
it has the smallest amount of contribution within a
firm's product portfolio do not clearly understand
this tool. Even the tiniest amount of contribution
can be used to pay towards the firm's fixed costs. By
contrast, discontinuing the product could mean less
total contribution and hence less overall profit for the
business.
Contribution costing also considers a firm's marginal cost.
This refers to the additional costs of producing an extra unit of
output. Understanding the marginal cost of production enables
a business to set an appropriate price to ensure it makes a
positive contribution from the sale of each product. The surplus
or positive contribution, is then used to pay towards the fixed
or indirect costs of production (see the worked example below).

Exam tip!
Worked Example
The costs incurred by a firm that produces hand-made
leather shoes are as follows:
Costs (per pair of shoes) $
Materials 15
Direct labour 20
Indirect costs 10
Total cost (per pair) 45
Calculate the marginal cost of producing an extra pair of
shoes.
Answer:
The marginal cost refers to the extra costs incurred
by producing an extra pair of shoes. Indirect costs are
excluded as they do not relate directly to the actual
output of the shoes. Hence, the marginal cost would be
$15 + $20 = $35. This means the shoes must be sold for
more than this price in order for the business to earn any
contribution towards paying its indirect costs.
Contribution and contribution pricing (see Chapter 28) are
also important for public sector for-profit social enterprises
(see Chapter 2). For example, state-owned enterprises are often
run as cost or profit centres, holding their management teams
accountable for the costs and/or revenues of each public sector
company.
However, the main limitation of contribution pricing is that it
is not always easy (or objective) to classify costs as either direct
or indirect (see Chapter 16).
Figure 57.3 - Is electricity a direct or indirect cost for
businesses?
Absorption costing

Absorption costing is an extension of contribution costing.
It involves deciding on the most appropriate way to apportion
(distribute or share out), a firm's indirect or fixed costs. This
helps to ensure that the price covers all costs of production (both
the direct costs and the apportioned costs). So, for example, in
the case of Cafe Cuppa, suppose the business has fixed costs of
$1,200 per month. A simple way to allocate these costs is to split
this equally (1,200 / 6 = $200 per product per month) so each
product absorbs the same amount of the fixed costs, as shown
in Table 57.2.

Evaluation of contribution

Contribution analysis has numerous uses for businesses:

Pricing strategy (see Chapter 28) - Contribution analysis
helps a business to set prices for each of its products to
ensure there is a positive contribution being made towards
Make or buy decisions (see above) - Contribution
analysis can help a business decide whether it should
produce (make) certain products or purchase them (buy)
from suppliers. The relative difference between the unit
contribution of making or buying the product is likely to
determine the decision.
payment of fixed and indirect costs. • Allocation of overheads to cost and profit centres (see
Product portfolio management (see Chapter 47) - The
analysis can help managers to decide which products should
be given priority for investment. In general, products with
a higher total contribution tend to be given precedence.
Chapter 22) - The use of contribution analysis can ensure
that cost allocations are done in a fair manner, based on
criteria that are clearly communicated to budget holders in
advance (see absorption costing above).

i.e., TC = TR. Break-even is a key objective of new and

However, contribution is only effective if the data used in
the analysis is accurate and up to date. Furthermore, cost
allocations need to be done in an open (transparent) and clearly

distort the outcomes of the analysis. Nevertheless, contribution

Increasing sales revenue, such as by using appropriate
pricing methods (see Chapter 28), improved promotional

Absorption costing involves deciding the most appropriate way
to apportion a firm's indirect or fixed costs between different
products and departments of the business to ensure that the
price covers all costs of production.
Contribution refers to the difference between the sales revenue
earned from selling a product (its price) and the variable costs
of producing the product.
Contribution costing is a method of valuing costs by allocating
direct costs to products or divisions (departments) of a business.
A make or buy decision refers to a situation where a business
has to decide whether to manufacture a product or to purchase

Simple linear regression

The Business Management toolkit is a set of
situational, planning and decision-making tools
used to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content
as well as being applied in different contexts. Simple
linear regression is a decision-making tool. The syllabus specifies
three types of simple aggression as part of the toolkit: (i) Scatter
diagrams, (ii) line of best lit and (iii) Correlation/Extrapolation.
© 180, 2022
S

imple linear regression is a statistical tool used to study
the nature of the relationships between two variables.
One of the variables is the independent variable (also
known as the predictor or explanatory) and the other one is the
dependent variable. For example, businesses might be interested
in knowing the relationship between their advertising spending
and the impact on the sales of their products. They might also
want to see how average incomes in the economy affect the
amount of consumer spending.

Given that most new products fail to get established on the
market (see Chapter 27), this implies that businesses often over-
predict their sales, i.e., sales forecasting (see Chapter 25) is not
an exact science and you need to be aware of the limitations.
Hence, managers also use simple regression analysis in order to
assist in making predictions and strategic decisions.

Figure 58.1 - Statistical tools are used to improve decision-
making in the workplace
As a quantitative tool, simple linear regression helps managers
and entrepreneurs by tackling issues of complexity, volatility,
ambiguity and uncertainty which are all associated with
business decision making. The 1B syllabus specifies three types
of simple aggression as part of the BMT: (i) scatter diagrams,
(ii) the line of best fit and (iii) correlation/extrapolation.
(i) Scatter diagrams
Scatter diagrams are a statistical visual tool that can be used
to show relationships between two different variables in a data
set, such as advertising spending and sales revenue. A scatter
diagram consists of data points that plot the values of one
variable on the x-axis (such as academic qualifications) and the
Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

other variable on the y-axis (such as the amount or value of an
employee's salary).

Relationships in a scatter diagram can fall into three categories:

A positive correlation means the two variables move in the
same direction in a scatter diagram, such as the demand
for complementary goods like shoes and socks or tennis
racquets and tennis balls.
A negative correlation means the two variables move in the
opposite direction in a scatter diagram, such as in the case
of substitute products, e.g., the price Coca-Cola and the
demand for Pepsi Cola.
Strong
Positive
Correlation
There is no correlation between the two variables if the data
sets do not show a positive or negative correlation, such as
the age of employees in an organization and how far they
have to travel in order to get to work.
In general, there are five types of patterns that tend to arise
from scatter diagrams, with the following descriptions for
each. In Figure 58.2, the data points are depicted as clouds for
illustrative purposes.

{ii} Line of best fit
A line of best fit (also known as the regression line) is a
statistical technique that involves calculating and drawing a
straight line that goes roughly through the middle of all the
points on a scatter diagram. The line of best fit helps to express
the relationship between the two variables shown in the scatter
graph. The closer the scatter points are to the line of best fit, the
stronger the correlation is between the two variables and vice
A strong correlation exists if the data in a scatter graph do not
deviate from the line of best fit by very much; the closer the data
points are to the regression line, the stronger the relationship
between the two variables being investigated. A moderate
correlation (positive or negative) exists if a line of best fit can be
determined but the data points are not always closely aligned
with the regression line.

(iii} Correlation/Extrapolation

Correlation indicates the extent to which there is a relationship
between two variables or events, such as sales revenue for
a product and different seasons of the year or the amount of
marketing expenditure and market share. So, for example, if
marketing executives and managers can identify a correlation
between advertising expenditure and consumer spending on
a particular good or service, they can take advantage of this
knowledge in order to further improve sales and ultimately
profits.

Extrapolation is a statistical technique that enables managers
to estimate data values beyond the original data set used as the
basis to determine the type of correlation. Extrapolation takes
the line of best fit one step further in simple linear regression
and is used as a prediction tool, as illustrated in Figure 58.3.

Time
Key
Actual sales \.J"
Trend -
Extrapolated
trend
Figure 58.3 - Extrapolation of sales trend
This forecasting technique identifies the trend by using past data
and extending this trend to predict future sales. For example, if
a firm's sale revenues have increased by an average of 5% each
year for the past several years, then it might be expected that
this trend continues in the near future. Graphically, the trend
can be shown by a line of best fit and extrapolation simply
extends this line to make predictions. Extrapolation works well
if there is a clear and strong correlation (relationship) between
two data sets.
.___ __

Business Management Toolkit (BMT)

However, correlation differs from causation, which indicates
that the occurrence of one event (such as greater expenditure
on staff training) has caused the occurrence of a second event
(such as improved productivity in the workplace). Whilst
correlation can explain causation, this is not necessarily the
case. As an example, statisticians have discovered that as ice
cream sales in Australia increase, the rate of shark attacks also
increases dramatically. However, this does not mean that ice
cream sales cause shark attacks - this would not make logical
sense. Statisticians explain this by going beyond the data
showing that on hotter days more people buy ice cream as well
as spending more time swimming in the sea so may be more
prone to shark attacks.
Exam tip!
For IB assessment purposes, the line of best fit should
be drawn through the scatter data points in a scatter
diagram to express the relationship between two
variables. You will not be expected to calculate the line
of best fit (regression line). Importantly, simple linear
regression is used as an estimation tool by managers,
such as using the line of best fit in a scatter diagram to
extrapolate (or predict) future outcomes.
Exam tip!
Remember that a correlation only shows if there is a
relationship between two variables in a data set. It does
not provide any insight into why such a relationship
might exist. Furthermore, correlation does not allow us
to go beyond the data that are given. Therefore, as with
all quantitative techniques in Business Management, be
careful with how you use data and interpret the findings.
Box 58.1 - Correlation, Causation or
Coincidence?
Vox Media reported that American residing in large
cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco in California
live longer.
The Journal of the American Medical Association
(JAMA) reported that Americans with higher incomes
have longer lives on average.
The New York Times reported a study that showed
sleeping in a room with a fan lowered a baby's
sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) by 72%.
Reuters Health reported that elderly people in the
UK with tooth loss are three times more prone to
memory loss caused by dementia.
The guardian newspaper reported that a study
showed feeding children with a healthy diet rich in
fish could prevent anti-social and violent behaviour
in their teen years.
The Harvard Business Review showed a close
correlation between the number of visitors to
Universal Orlando's "Islands of Adventure"theme park
with the sales of new cars in the US.
The US Department of Agriculture and National
Science Foundation revealed a 95.86% correlation
between the consumption of mozzarella cheese
and the number of Engineering Doctorate (EngD)
qualifications awarded.
Data from US Census and United States Department
of Agriculture showed a 99% correlation between the
consumption of margarine and the divorce rates in
the state of Maine.
Exam tip!
For IB assessment purposes, be prepared to comment
on the nature of the correlation by using a line of best
fit. You will need to comment on whether the data show
there is a positive, negative or no correlation between
the variables.

Evaluation of simple linear
regression
As with any quantitative or statistical tool, the benefits of using
simple linear regression will depend on the validity of the data
collected and used to calculate correlations and trends. Whilst
linear regression can help to minimise the risks of decision
making, you need to be aware of the potential limitations behind
the data. In particular, the line of best fit can be easily distorted
by random variations and outliers in data sets (see Box 58.2).
The prolonged COVID-19 pandemic, for example, will have
distorted data sets for businesses across all industries in every
part of the world. Seasonal fluctuations in demand for certain
goods and services can also create challenges in determining
relationships and correlations (see Box 58.3).

Figure 58.4 - The COVID-19 pandemic has made linear
regression analysis less reliable
Finally, it is important to remember that correlation does
not always imply causation, irrespective of what the linear
regression data might show. After all, a set of data conceals as
much information as it reveals.

KEY TERMS
Correlation indicates the extent to which there is a relationship
between two variables or events e.g., the amount of marketing
expenditure and market share.

Extrapolation is a statistical technique that enables managers
to estimate data values beyond the original data set used as the
basis to determine the type of correlation.

A line of best fit is a statistical technique that involves calculating
and drawing a straight line that goes roughly through the middle
of all the points on a scatter graph. It is used to determine the
relationship, if any, between two variables under investigation.

Scatter diagrams are a statistical visual tool that can be used to
show relationship between two different variables in a data set.

Simple linear regression is a statistical Business Management
tool used to study the nature of the relationships between two
variables.

Introducing the key concepts in Business

Management

"The world is moving at a tremendous rate. Going no one knows where. We must prepare our children, not for the world of
the past. Not for our world. But for their world. The world of the future."
John Dewey (1859-1952), American educational leader, philosopher and psychologist
What is concept-based learning?

Concept-based learning
(CBL), as defined by
education consultant
Dr. H. Lynn Erickson, is
of learning that frames
facts (content) and skills
with key concepts and
understanding in the
Business Management
course. The rigour of
the course creates two
approaches to teaching
and learning: either students can be told what they need to
know (based on factual knowledge and skills in Business
Management) or teachers can get their students excited enough
to discover and deepen their understanding of Business
Management for themselves.

Concepts are large, interdisciplinary ideas that have relevance
both within and across academic subject areas. They help
to move students from content-based knowledge to deeper
understandings by using conceptual lenses that facilitate the
transfer of knowledge across subject content and contexts. The
IB uses a concept-based approach to teaching and learning.
In Business Management, the four prescribed concepts are
change, ethics, sustainability and creativity.

The 21st Century learner lives in a mobile and digital world
with access to growing facts and information at their fingertips.
As educators, we cannot expect our students to learn (just)
more content knowledge in Business Management. Instead, we
have to help students to connect the factual knowledge to more

permanent (timeless) and interdisciplinary concepts to advance
their knowledge and understandings. In Business Management,
concepts are used to give students the tools necessary to make
sense of the world. Supporters of CBL argue that it is through
these conceptual lenses that learning truly begins to make sense
for students.
Concept-based learning is not about learning facts and figures
in isolation. Instead, it is about encouraging students to:
Think beyond the factual contents of the Business
Management course.
Be active learners rather than passive learners (for example,
there is huge scope in Business Management to use inquiry
to engage students in their learning).
Be inquiring and curious learners who want to further their
understanding and knowledge (such as through the use of
real-world case studies that students are interested in).
Make connections of knowledge in Business Management
to the key concepts as transferable ideas or lenses across all
topics in the course.
Apply their knowledge and thinking to solve problems
using an organized framework (the four key concepts of
change, creativity, ethics and sustainability).
Use multiple sources and media to gain and extend
knowledge and understanding, as well as to recognise the
transferability of knowledge to familiar and unfamiliar
situations.
Supplementary information

Think critically and creatively to solve problems.
Discuss and collaborate with peers to progress their own
learning.
Organise and make sense of their own learning.
Own and drive their own learning in a synergistic way.
Hence, CBL can help students to broaden their knowledge
and understanding of the world around them (see Table 53.1).
Essentially, concept-based teaching and learning are integral to
the IB's teaching and learning pedagogy
